en: The Sutra on the Unprecedented Causes and Conditions Spoken by the Buddha, Volume One.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Tanjing of the Xiao Qi Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maudgalyāyana:

"Go now to the city of Kapilavastu to inquire after my father, King Śuddhodana, as well as my maternal aunt Mahāprajāpatī and my three uncles, including King Droṇodana. Furthermore, console Rāhula’s mother, Yaśodharā, and cause her to sever her bonds of affection so that she may release Rāhula, allowing him to become a śrāmaṇera and cultivate the Noble Path."

Why is this so? The affection between mother and child brings joy for but a moment; yet when death occurs and one falls into hell, mother and child will no longer know one another. In the profound darkness, they shall be parted forever, suffering myriad forms of misery beyond remedy through regret.
If Rāhula attains the Way, he shall return to deliver his mother, eternally severing the root of birth, old age, sickness, and death, and reaching Nirvāṇa, just as I have now.

Maudgalyāyana accepted the command and immediately entered meditative concentration. In the time it takes a strong man to bend or extend his arm, he arrived at Kapilavastu at the residence of King Śuddhodana and addressed the king, saying:
"The World-Honored One sends you his most earnest greetings; he asks whether your daily life is light and easy, and whether your strength and health are secure."
The Chief Queen Māyādevī, along with her three paternal uncles, King Droṇodana and the others, likewise inquired after his well-being in the same manner.
At that time, Yaśodharā heard that the Buddha had sent a messenger to the king’s palace; not yet knowing his purpose, she immediately dispatched a maidservant to inquire about the news.
The maidservant returned and reported:
"The World-Honored One has sent a messenger to take Rāhula and ordain him as a śrāmaṇera.
Upon hearing this news, Yaśodharā took Rāhula up to a high tower and commanded the supervising officials to close all doors and gates, ensuring they were all made secure.

At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana arrived at the palace gate but was unable to enter, as no one would admit him. He then used his supernormal powers to fly up to a high tower and stood before Yaśodharā’s seat.

When Yaśodharā saw Maudgalyāyana approaching, her heart was filled with a mixture of sorrow and joy; constrained by necessity, she immediately rose with reverence, prostrated, and inquired after his well-being:
"Having traveled such a long distance, I hope you have not been fatigued?"
He ordered a seat to be prepared and invited Maudgalyāyana to sit.
He asked Maudgalyāyana:
"Is the World-Honored One free from ailment? In teaching and transforming sentient beings, does he not weary his spirit?"
“Why have you sent this superior man here? What do you intend to do?
Maudgalyāyana replied, “Prince Rāhula is now nine years old; he should be permitted to leave the household life and cultivate the Noble Path.”

Why is this so? The affection between mother and child may be as one wishes for a short time, but once life ends, they fall into the three evil realms; their love and separation become profound and dark, such that the mother knows not her son and the son knows not his mother.

Yet Rāhula has attained the Way and shall return to deliver his mother, forever crossing over birth, old age, sickness, death, and the afflictions of grief, until he reaches Nirvāṇa, just as the Buddha does now.
Yaśodharā replied to Maudgalyāyana:

"When Śākyamuni Tathāgata was a prince, he took me as his wife. I served the prince as if serving a celestial deity, never committing even a single transgression. Before three years had passed since we became husband and wife, he abandoned the pleasures of the five desires, leaped over the palace walls, and fled to the royal fields."
The King went in person to welcome him back, but he was obstinate and would not comply; he then sent Chandaka and the white horse back, vowing that he would only return once his Way was perfected.

Clad in deerskin, like a madman, he lived in seclusion among the mountains and marshes for six years of arduous toil. Having attained Buddhahood, he returned to the kingdom but did not see his kin; he forgot and neglected his old bonds of affection, treating them worse than strangers. Separated from his parents, he dwells in another land, leaving us, mother and son, to endure solitude and poverty with no means of livelihood, save for death itself.

Human life is most precious; one cannot inflict injury upon oneself. To harbor malice and resentment while forcibly clinging to existence—though classified among the human race, such a person is no better than a beast. Among all calamities, how could there be anything more grievous than this?
Now you have sent an envoy again, wishing to seek my son to be his retinue; how can this be so cruel?
The Prince attained the Way and spoke of himself as compassionate and merciful;
yet the Way of compassion and mercy should bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, yet now it instead causes the separation of mother and child.
"Among all sufferings, none is more severe than the suffering of being separated from those one loves; reasoning from this, what compassion can there be?
He said to Maudgalyāyana, "Please convey what I have related to the World-Honored One."
Then Mahāmaudgalyāyana again employed various skillful means and diverse causes and conditions to offer admonitions and exhortations as appropriate, repeating them two or three times.
Yet Yaśodharā remained utterly unwilling to listen; she took her leave and returned to King Śuddhodana, reporting the matter in full detail.
Having heard this, the King ordered the summoning of Queen Māyādevī and said to her:
"My son Siddhārtha has sent Maudgalyāyana to fetch Rāhula, desiring that he enter the religious life to cultivate and study the Noble Dharma."

Yaśodharā is a woman of ignorance who has not yet understood the essential points of the Dharma; her mind is firm and her will resolute as she remains entangled in affection and love, with no thought of relinquishing her feelings.
You should go to her and earnestly exhort and apologize to her, so that her heart may attain awakening.

Thereupon, the chief queen immediately took five hundred maidservants in blue garments and went to the palace where Yaśodharā resided; she exhorted and admonished her with various skillful means as appropriate, repeating this two or three times.
Yaśodharā still would not listen, and she said to her mother-in-law:
"When I was at home, the kings of the eight nations vied with one another to come and ask for my hand in marriage, yet my parents did not grant their permission."
Why is this? Prince Śākyamuni’s talents and skills surpass those of men; for this reason, my parents betrothed me to him.
Since the Prince already knew at that time that he would not remain in the world but would leave home to study the Way, why did he so earnestly and painfully seek me out?

When a man takes a wife, it is precisely for the sake of affection and harmony, so that they may gather in joy and prosperity, passing it down through ten thousand generations, with sons and grandsons continuing in succession to uphold the ancestral lineage. This is the proper rite of the world. Now that the Crown Prince has already departed, why do you further seek Rāhula and desire him to renounce the world, thereby forever severing the royal succession? What meaning is there in this?
At that time, having heard these words, the Queen remained silent and speechless, not knowing what to say.
Then the World-Honored One immediately dispatched a manifested being who spoke from mid-air, saying: "Yaśodharā!
"Do you perhaps remember the matter of your vow in a former age?

At that time, when Śākyamuni Tathāgata was practicing the path of a bodhisattva, he purchased five stalks of lotus flowers from you for five hundred silver coins and offered them to Dīpaṃkara Buddha."
At that time, you sought me out, saying that in every life we were born together as husband and wife.
I did not wish to accept this, and I spoke to you, saying:
"I am a Bodhisattva; throughout successive kalpas, I have practiced my vows and given all things in charity, never refusing the wishes of others."
"If you can do this, I grant that you shall be my wife.
You then made this vow:

"In every lifetime in which we are born, whether it be kingdoms, cities, wives, children, or even my own body, I shall give them away to you as you see fit; I swear that I shall never harbor a heart of regret."
"But for what reason do you now cherish Rāhula and not allow him to leave the household life to study the Noble Path?

When Yaśodharā heard these words, she suddenly regained her memory of the causes and conditions of her past karma; the events of her former life became as clear as if she had seen them yesterday. Her maternal affection for her son naturally subsided, and she sent for Maudgalyāyana to offer repentance and apologies, then took Rāhula’s hand and entrusted him to Maudgalyāyana.
As we part from you, our tears flow together.
At that time, seeing his mother’s sorrow and distress, Rāhula knelt down with palms joined and addressed her in farewell:
“I pray that you do not grieve; Rāhula shall now go to pay his respects to the World-Honored One.”
"Before long, he shall return and meet with his mother.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, wishing to comfort Yaśodharā and bring her joy, immediately summoned the prominent families of the kingdom and addressed them, saying:
"The Prince of the Golden Wheel is now to depart for the kingdom of Śrāvastī to leave the household life and study the Way under the Buddha, the World-Honored One."
"I request that you each send one son to follow my grandson.
They all replied, "So be it."
"I obey the Great King's command.
Immediately, fifty men gathered together and followed Rāhula to the place where the Buddha was, prostrating themselves with their heads at his feet.
The Buddha then instructed Ānanda to shave the heads of Rāhula and those fifty princes, and he caused them all to go forth into homelessness.
Śāriputra was appointed as his upādhyāya and Mahāmaudgalyāyana served as his ācārya; they conferred upon him the ten precepts, and he thus became a śrāmaṇera.
Because Rāhula was young, he was accustomed to being arrogant and indulged in play, taking no pleasure in listening to the Dharma.
The Buddha had repeatedly admonished him, yet he never followed his instructions; there was nothing that could be done about it.

At that time, King Prasenajit of Śrāvastī, having heard that the Buddha’s son Rāhula had left home to become a śrāmaṇera, came to the Buddha’s dwelling at dawn accompanied by his ministers, queens, crown prince, palace ladies, brahmins, and lay devotees. Surrounded by them in respectful attendance, he paid homage and inquired after the Buddha’s well-being, and together with them, came to see the Buddha’s son, the śrāmaṇera Rāhula. They each sat to one side, and the Buddha preached the Dharma for them.
The king and his ministers, being arrogant and accustomed to pleasure, were unable to endure sitting in discomfort to hear the Buddha’s teaching; they took their leave, intending to return.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the king had only just begun to awaken but that the faculty of faith was not yet established, and wishing to bring enlightenment to the king and his ministers for their benefit, addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should go and summon the śrāmaṇera Rāhula and his retinue, and have them all assemble to hear the Buddha’s teaching."
Ānanda went to summon them, and in a short while they had all assembled.
The Buddha said to the king,
"Wait a moment and listen as I preach the Dharma."
The king joined his palms and said, “My body has long been accustomed to pleasure; I am unable to endure sitting in this painful posture. I pray that the Buddha will grant me his forgiveness.
The Buddha told the king:
"This is not suffering. Why is that?

Because in a previous life he planted merit, he is now a king of men, constantly dwelling in the deep palace with the five desires at his disposal; when he goes out or comes in, he is escorted by attendants so that his feet do not touch the ground—how can this be called suffering?"

"Among the sufferings of the three realms, none are equal to those of hell, the animal realm, the hungry ghosts, and the various calamities; such sufferings as these have already been explained previously.
The Buddha told Rāhula:
"A Buddha’s world is difficult to encounter, the Dharma is difficult to hear, human life is difficult to preserve, and attaining the Way is likewise difficult."
"Now that you have obtained a human body and encountered a Buddha during his lifetime, for what reason are you indolent and do not listen to the Dharma?
Rāhula addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Buddha’s Dharma is subtle and wondrous, but my mind as a child is coarse; how could I possibly receive and uphold the World-Honored One’s Dharma?"
I have already heard this many times before, yet I immediately forget it again; thus I have merely exhausted my spirit without gaining anything at all.
Now that I am still young, I shall indulge my passions and follow my whims; when I reach old age, I will naturally be somewhat improved and capable of receiving the Dharma.
The Buddha said to Rāhula:
"All things are impermanent, and even this body is difficult to preserve. Are you able to guarantee that your life will last until you reach adulthood?
"Indeed, World-Honored One! [Rāhula replied.]
"Rāhula cannot; how could the Buddha not be able to protect his son's life?
The Buddha said to Rāhula:
“I cannot even preserve myself; how could I preserve you?
Rāhula addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is all in vain to listen to the Dharma. Since I have not attained the Way, what benefit does the merit of hearing the Dharma bring to a person?”
The Buddha told Rāhula:
"As for the merit of listening to the Dharma, even if one cannot attain the Way in this present life, it will bring great benefit throughout many future births within the five realms of existence."
As I have previously stated, the wisdom of *prajñā* is also called nectar, also called a fine medicine, also called a bridge, and also called a great ship; have you not heard this?
Rāhula addressed the Buddha:
“Indeed it is so,
World-Honored One!”
At that time, King Prasenajit knelt with his right knee on the ground and joined his palms, addressing the World-Honored One:
“As the Buddha has taught, there are four names for the wisdom of *prajñā*; what is their meaning?”
"I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will explain this for me.
The Buddha said to the king, "If you wish to hear it, listen attentively with a focused mind; I shall now speak of it."
The Buddha said:

"Recall that in the past, countless kalpas ago, there was a jackal in Mount Xitada in the great kingdom of Vimala. A lion king pursued it, intending to devour it; terrified, the jackal fled and fell into a pit on a mound. Unable to escape, it remained there for three days until its heart broke and it was on the verge of death, whereupon it spoke this verse:
'Alas! Today I am oppressed by suffering; I shall surely lose my life in this pit on the mound.'"
All things in the universe are impermanent; I regret not having fed my body to the lions.
Alas, what can be done with this body burdened by sin and calamity?
To die without merit while greedily cherishing one's life—death without merit is already lamentable, how much more so when this stinking body defiles the waters of others!
Homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions; I confess my transgressions, manifesting that my mind is pure and without end.
For the sins of the three karmas committed in previous lives, I vow to repay them fully within this present body.
All sins being exhausted, the three karmas are purified; with a mind unmoving, one contemplates the truth.
From this point on, life after life, one encounters enlightened teachers and, practicing according to the Dharma, swiftly attains Buddhahood.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, hearing the name of the Buddha, was struck with solemn awe such that his hair stood on end as he recalled the Buddhas of antiquity.
He reflected upon himself: "I am solitary and exposed, lacking a teacher or guide;
I am addicted to the five desires and have sunk into them myself, unable to escape the prison of affection and craving. Contemplating this with poignant emotion, tears fell from his eyes.
Immediately, accompanied by a multitude of eighty thousand devas, he flew down to the well to offer his greetings.
There he saw a jackal at the bottom of the well, clinging with both paws to the earth, unable to emerge.
The Lord of Devas then reflected to himself, saying:
"The Sage manifests in manifold ways; though I now see you in the form of a jackal, you must surely be a Bodhisattva and no ordinary vessel.
I shall now ask your questions to dispel my doubts, so that all the devas may likewise hear the Dharma."
The Lord of Devas said:
"It has been a long time since we have heard the vast and sublime teachings of the Sage; we have constantly dwelt in darkness without a teacher to guide us.
What you have just spoken, O Benevolent One, is no ordinary speech; we pray that you will proclaim the Dharma for the sake of all the devas."
At that time, the jackal looked up and replied:
"You do not know the propriety of the occasion; you are utterly foolish and arrogant. While the Dharma Master stands below, you place yourself above him;
you do not cultivate respect or inquire about the essentials of the Dharma. The water of the Dharma is pure and can save all people."
How can one who desires to harbor pride expect the various devas to serve him?
They will stare in astonishment and laugh; even the descent of the Heavenly King brings no great benefit, yet to be subjected to such shame is truly pitiable.
Śakra immediately addressed the devas:
"Be careful not to regard this as a cause for alarm or wonder; it is because my own conduct has been dull and unworthy that I shall surely, by means of this, hear the essential Dharma."
I received the jackal and brought it out above; with palms joined in reverence, I apologized and confessed my error, prostrating myself in repentance and praying for your understanding:
"I was entangled in the five desires until I fell into confusion and ruin; all this was due to not having encountered a virtuous teacher to guide me."
He preached for them on suffering and happiness, permanence and impermanence.
The jackal, having obtained food for its livelihood, did not expect such fortune amidst calamity;
its heart leaped with joy at this immeasurable celebration.
Thereupon, the jackal thought to himself:
"Within the realm of animals, there is no one more ugly, wretched, and distressed than a jackal;
yet, by the power of wisdom, I have attained such a state."
Again, he thought to himself:
"A life of mutilation and suffering is fundamentally not something to be cherished; the reason I celebrate and feel such great joy is solely for the sake of promoting transformation."
"These foolish devas all possess a single hair’s breadth of the portion of *prajñā* that Śakra previously held; they have come together with him, desiring to hear the Dharma.
Then he sighed to himself, saying:
"How marvelous, how marvelous!"
"What consolation could equal this? Now that the transformation shall be communicated, shall it not fulfill my merit? He further thought:
"Is today’s grace not entirely due to the compassionate instruction and the power of the wisdom, skillful means, and merit of my former teacher, the Upādhyāya?"
Homage to my Teacher, homage to my Teacher; homage to Prajñā, homage to Prajñā.
Although they may lose their practice and be reborn in the evil realms, they still remember their past lives and understand the karmic conditions thereof.

"By the power of Prajñā, he is able to move the various devas to descend and manifest their spirits, providing succor and offerings, and further attaining spiritual transformations to expand my humble mind.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, said to the devas:
"If it is as the Master says, he certainly intends to preach the Dharma."
"We have now come and swiftly obtained great benefit; we shall now each prostrate ourselves with sincere devotion and entreat you to preach the Dharma.
All agreed, saying "Yes," and immediately paid their respects. Baring their right shoulders, they circled the jackal, knelt with palms joined, and spoke these verses in one voice:
"Excellent, excellent!..."
O Upādhyāya, we pray that you preach the Dharma to transform and enlighten gods and humans.
We constantly fear that our merit will be exhausted and that we shall be swept away by impermanence, falling into the evil realms at death;
it would be most difficult to seek deliverance from there. Since time immemorial, for tens of thousands of millions of years, [we have wandered].
Now, having met for the first time this excellent field of merit, may you deign to show compassion and proclaim the words of the Dharma;
thus gods and humans shall obtain blessings, and all sentient beings likewise.
I pray that I may be linked with the Upādhyāya through eternal kalpas, until we together attain the Way of Buddhahood.
"Always create the causes and conditions;
for wise people are difficult to encounter, therefore I have established this vow.
Thereupon, seeing that the devas and humans earnestly entreated him and were eager to hear the Dharma, the jackal was filled with even greater joy and addressed the Lord of Devas, saying:

"I recall that in the past, when I saw people of the world who wished to hear the Dharma, they would first prepare a high seat, adorning it with purity, and only then invite the Dharma Master to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma."
"Why is this? Because the sutras and the Dharma are precious; by honoring them one gains merit, so one should not treat them with a frivolous mind, thereby diminishing one's own merit.

When the devas heard this, they all assented with "So be it. They removed their celestial jeweled robes and piled them up to form a high seat; in an instant, it was adorned and decorated until it was the most pure and magnificent of all.
The jackal ascended the seat and addressed the Lord of Devas, saying:
"I shall now preach the Dharma specifically for two great causes and conditions. What are these two?"
"First, because preaching the Dharma to enlighten and transform devas and humans brings immeasurable merit;
second, because it is to repay the kindness of those who provide food, how could one not preach?
The Heavenly Emperor said:
"Having escaped the peril of the well and preserved one's body and life, the merit [thereof] ought to be great.
Why is it that the Venerable One’s teaching on repaying kindness does not equal this?"
Why is this so? Because throughout the entire world, all beings delight in life, seek security, and have no desire for death.
For these reasons, how could the merit of preserving one's life not be considered great?
The jackal replied:
"Regarding the propriety of life and death, each person has their own disposition; some people crave life, while others delight in death.
Who is it that craves life?"

Such a person is born into this world ignorant and shrouded in darkness; they do not know that after death one is reborn in a future life. They turn away from the Buddha and distance themselves from the Dharma, failing to encounter an enlightened teacher. They engage in killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and deception, following only in evil.
Such a person craves life and fears death.
Who would delight in death?

Having encountered an enlightened teacher, they serve the Triple Gem, reform their evils and cultivate goodness, provide filial support for their parents, respectfully attend to their teachers and elders, live in harmony with their wives, children, servants, and kin, and show humility and respect toward others.
Such a person as this would rather suffer evil than experience death.
Why is this? Because when a virtuous person dies, their merit should lead them to be born in heaven to enjoy the pleasures of the five senses.
When an evil person dies, they should enter hell to undergo immeasurable suffering.
A good person delights in death, like a prisoner released from jail;
an evil person fears death, like a prisoner entering a jail.
The Heavenly Emperor asked:
"As Your Reverence has taught, it is indeed as you say that there is no merit in merely preserving one's own body and life.
As for the other two merits—giving food and giving the Dharma—what kind of merit do they possess?"
"I only pray that you will explain this, so as to enlighten and transform those who are blind and ignorant.

The jackal replied, "Giving food and drink merely sustains life for a single day; giving precious treasures merely sustains the blessings of a single lifetime; both increase the causes and conditions for the bondage of birth and death."
To preach the Dharma and provide instruction is called the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*);
it can cause sentient beings to enter the supramundane path. There are three kinds of supramundane paths:
first, the path of the Arhat; second, that of the Pratyekabuddha; and third, the path of the Buddha.
These followers of the three vehicles all attain their goals by hearing the Dharma and practicing according to its teachings.
There are sentient beings who escape the three evil realms and receive the blessings and joys of humans and devas; all of this is due to hearing the Dharma.
"Therefore, the Buddha has said that the merit of giving the Dharma as a gift is immeasurable.
The Heavenly Emperor addressed him, saying:
"Is this present body of the Master one born of karmic retribution, or is it a response-body or transformation-body?"
The jackal replied, "This is the retribution for sinful karma; it is not a manifestation through transformation.

Upon hearing this, the devas and humans were struck with solemn awe and terror; their hearts were pained with sorrow, and tears flowed down to fill their eyes. Rising once more to pay their respects, they addressed the jackal, saying:
"In my mind, I thought this Bodhisattva was a holy being manifesting to save sentient beings; yet now I hear of the retribution for sinful karma.
I do not know the reason for this; I only pray that you will take pity on me and explain its causes and conditions."
The jackal replied: "It is well that you wish to hear; I shall now speak of it.
Recalling my former existence, I was born in the city of Pāṭaliputra in Vārāṇasī as the son of a poor family, named Ajita, of the Kṣatriya caste."
From childhood he possessed keen intelligence and a desire for learning.
At the age of twelve, he followed a wise teacher into the deep mountains, where he served him with diligence, refining his studies through tireless effort.

The teacher, in turn, instructed him morning and night, never missing the proper timing for cultivation. After fifty years, he had attained mastery in all fields, including the ninety-six kinds of scriptures, records, and treatises, as well as medical prescriptions, incantations, divination of good and bad fortune, and the interpretation of portents and calamities.
Possessing lofty talent, wisdom, and virtue, his fame spread far and wide.
At that time, Ajita reflected within himself, saying:
"The salvation I have attained today is entirely due to the grace of my honored teacher and preceptor’s instruction; his merit is difficult to repay."
"Since my family is impoverished and has nothing with which to provide offerings, I must sell my own body to repay the kindness of my teacher.
Having formed this thought, he knelt for a long time and said to his teacher:
"I, your disciple, now wish to sell my own body to repay the kindness of my teacher."
The master replied:
"I am a mountain-dwelling practitioner who sustains myself by begging for food; I truly lack nothing.
Why do you now ruin and sell your noble body, wishing to provide for me?"

You have now perfected wisdom and eloquence; you should go forth to transform and teach the people of the world. By acting as a lamp of the Dharma, will not the merit of your teaching be sufficient to repay my kindness?
"I am fortunate that there is no need for any further exertion.
At that time, Ajita, being a man of wisdom, did not disobey his teacher's instruction and remained in the mountains, sustaining himself by begging for alms.

"Thus, before long, the king passed away. The ministers gathered to deliberate and issued a proclamation throughout the realm, summoning all renowned scholars to assemble together for a debate. 'Whosoever emerges victorious shall be established as king.'"
At that time, Ajita was summoned and assembled; together with more than five hundred scholars, they debated and contended for seven days, yet none emerged victorious.
The ministers rejoiced and summoned the brahmin, installing Ajita as the king.
Upon witnessing this event, Ajita was filled with a mixture of sorrow and joy, and he thought to himself:

"If I become a king, I fear I will fall into arrogance and excess, greedily seeking pleasure and thereby bringing calamity upon the people; after death, I shall enter hell and experience the causes and conditions of suffering."
"If I do not do so, my family will remain poor and without means, leaving me unable to provide for them or repay the profound kindness of my teacher.
After reflecting on this repeatedly, he thought, "I shall accept it, so as to repay my teacher’s kindness and support my parents."
Having reflected thus, he accepted the royal throne.

Once he had assumed the position of sovereign, he immediately dispatched loyal ministers to prepare a precious chariot adorned with banners, streamers, and curved parasols, along with fragrant flowers, music, and a hundred varieties of food and drink, to go to the mountain and welcome the Master back to the kingdom to provide him with offerings.

He constructed a separate palace, inlaid with the seven treasures and adorned with intricate carvings, engravings, and various colorful decorations. It was furnished with beds, bedding, food, drink, medicine, flower gardens, fruit groves, flowing springs, and bathing pools—all exquisitely ornamented and magnificent—to provide for the service of his teacher.
King Ajita, together with the ministers and citizens of his realm, his queen, and his court ladies, daily received the ten wholesome precepts from his teacher for a period of one hundred years.

"At that time, there were two small kingdoms on the frontier—the kings of these two small kingdoms harbored mutual resentment and hostility; they raised private armies to attack and punish one another, and though many years passed, neither could prevail over the other.
One kingdom was named Andhra; the other was named Mālava."
King Andhra summoned his various ministers and assembled them to deliberate together, saying:
"What means should be employed to seize that kingdom?
The ministers replied:

“King Ajita was born into a humble and lowly station; though he occupied the throne, his sense of humility remained. Since ancient times, he has upheld the ten wholesome paths of action and refrained from violating the wives of others. Although he possesses palace women, they are all advanced in years.”

According to my plan, Your Majesty should conduct a census throughout the kingdom, regardless of noble or humble status, to select one hundred renowned women who are young, upright, and capable of pleasing the mind; they shall then be adorned with fragrant purity.
Dispatch loyal and virtuous men to carry precious treasures and various court ladies to present as tribute.
If he accepts them, you should request from the King a million strong troops to assist in attacking him; there is no place that will not submit.
He immediately followed that plan; having prepared the women and precious objects all at once, he dispatched a loyal and virtuous minister to present them as an offering.
Upon receiving the beautiful women and rare treasures, King Aviddha was greatly delighted and asked the messenger:
"That king has presented me with such excellent goods; what reward does he hope for?"
The messenger addressed the king, saying:

"The kingdom of Mālava is under Your Majesty's dominion; yet its king is obstinate and foolish, ignorant of how to transform and guide his people. He is licentious and lacks the Way, neglecting the administration of state affairs. The people suffer from his poison and regard him as an enemy."
"I have specifically requested a hundred thousand troops from Your Majesty to assist in subduing him.
My sincerity in this offering lies precisely here.
The King said, "Excellent," and immediately ordered the selection of one hundred thousand elite and powerful soldiers to be sent to him.
King Andhra personally selected one million men from within his kingdom; they assisted him all at once as he went forth to wage war with drums beating.
Within a hundred days, through the wounding and killing of battle, more than half of the men had died before he finally achieved victory over them.

King Mālava was completely executed, and his kinsmen numbering several tens of millions perished all at once. "Once King Aśvada had obtained the maidens, his mind became deluded and his passions confounded;

he forgot his original resolve and, indulging in luxury and lust, neglected the administration of state affairs. The various officials and ministers conspired together to rebel; the sons of the virtuous people were seized and made into slaves. Wind and rain did not come at their proper times, hunger filled the roads, and enemies from foreign lands subsequently came to invade and plunder."
King Ajita lost his kingdom from this point on and eventually met his end.

After dying, he was reborn in hell, where his body was subjected to agonizing torments; however, by virtue of the power of the wisdom he had previously cultivated through study, he immediately recognized his past lives, felt remorse and self-reproach in his heart, and reformed his evil ways to practice virtue.
In a mere moment, his life in hell came to an end, and he was reborn among the hungry ghosts (preta).
Again, he remembered his past lives and immediately repented, cultivating mindfulness of the ten wholesome actions.
In another brief instant, he died among the hungry ghosts and was reborn among the animals, receiving the body of a jackal.

By the power of wisdom, they further recognize their past lives, reforming their past and cultivating the future; they uphold the ten wholesome paths of action and further teach other sentient beings to practice these ten wholesome paths.
Recently I encountered a lion; at that time, out of fear, I fell into a mountain well. With my heart laid bare and facing death, I hoped to be reborn in heaven to escape suffering and enjoy bliss.
Because you rescued me, I have failed to fulfill my original vow; I must now endure hardship—when shall I ever be delivered from it?
"Therefore, I say that you have done me no service in saving my life.
The Heavenly Emperor (Śakra) challenged him, saying:
"According to your words, it would follow that a virtuous person seeks death; this is not so."
Why is this? The teacher is at the bottom of the well; if he does not enter the garment, he cannot emerge, and if he cannot emerge, he cannot be born.
That one now attains birth through conditions is due to the teacher having entered the garment.
"Therefore, you should know that it is not that they do not wish to be born.
Why, then, do you say they do not crave birth? The jackal replied:
"The reason I have now entered this robe is precisely for the sake of three great causes and conditions.
What are these three?
First, by entering the robe, I shall not contravene the original vows and aspirations of the Heavenly Emperor."
When a person’s will is thwarted and their wishes are not fulfilled, they experience great suffering and inflict distress upon others.
In every place where they are born, their desires remain unfulfilled, what they seek remains unattained, and their endeavors meet with failure; thus, they bring suffering upon themselves.
It is for the sake of these beings, and not for the sake of birth.

Second, he enters the robes to perceive the intentions of the devas; desiring to hear the Dharma and wishing to proclaim and disseminate the True Dharma for the sake of the devas, he does so out of non-stinginess regarding the Dharma.

If one does not speak [the Dharma], it constitutes stinginess regarding the Dharma. The transgression of stinginess regarding the Dharma results in being born deaf, blind, mute, or dumb, with the sensory faculties obstructed, in borderlands, or as a fool devoid of wisdom, in every lifetime one is reborn into.
Even if born in a favorable place, one’s disposition will be stubborn, dull, and obtuse, such that what is studied is not mastered.
Because learning is not mastered, one brings suffering and affliction upon oneself.
It is for the sake of these [beings] that [the Buddha appears], not for the sake of his own birth.

For example, just as people in the world, due to the causes and conditions of their merit from practicing charity and cultivating goodness in previous lives, are born as humans in this life with their wishes fulfilled by heart and possessed of abundant wealth.

When the poor beg for alms, those with stingy and parsimonious minds refuse to give. As the karmic retribution for such greed and avarice, they are born among the hungry ghosts (*preta*). They constantly suffer from hunger and thirst; they are naked and without clothing. In winter, their bodies crack and split from the freezing cold; in summer, they endure intense heat with no place of shelter. Such are their afflictions for many tens of millions of years.

When their retribution as hungry ghosts is exhausted, they are born among the animals; they eat grass and drink water, being ignorant and devoid of understanding. Some eat mud, filth, or impurities; because of the sins of stinginess and greed, they receive such retribution.
The transgression of being stingy with the Dharma is likewise the same.

Thirdly, as for entering [the assembly] wearing robes, it is precisely for the purpose of proclaiming and spreading the transformative teachings of the Dharma; because it benefits devas and humans by causing them to attain awakening, it is called the "gift of Dharma," and its merit is immeasurable.
"For the sake of those such as these, it is not for the purpose of seeking birth. The Heavenly Lord asked:
"Regarding the merit of teaching and transforming others, what is its blessing like?"
"I only pray that you will explain this. The jackal replied,

"To proclaim the true transformation is to enable sentient beings to know that death is followed by birth, that performing good brings forth blessings, that committing evil incurs calamity, and that practicing the Way leads to the attainment of the Way."
By virtue of this merit, in whatever body he is reborn, his wisdom will be clear and lucid, and he will always possess the knowledge of past lives.
If born in the heavens, he will become a teacher for the devas;
if born in the human world, he will become a Golden Wheel-turning King, constantly teaching and transforming the world through the ten wholesome paths of action.
If one becomes a king of men and governs by the True Dharma, one will constantly remember past lives.
Because of this recollection of past lives, the mind remains free from negligence.

When a person dwells in honor and receives the pleasures of the five desires, many demonic obstacles arise to obstruct and destroy them, causing the mind to become deluded and leading to the commission of evil karma.
Although they may fail in their practice and undergo the retribution of evil, by the power of wisdom they will swiftly escape suffering.

Reborn in heaven with its blessings and joys, the light of their wisdom will gradually increase, enabling them to fulfill the bodhisattva practices and attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
"Therefore, the Buddha has said that the merit of the work of teaching and transforming others is immeasurable.
The Heavenly Lord said joyfully,
"Excellent, excellent!"
It is exactly as your venerable teaching states.
Today, we gods have for the first time come to understand the distinct characteristics of the causes and conditions of the merit of material giving and the merit of Dharma giving.
Material giving is, for example, like a single-inch lamp illuminating a small room.
This gift of Dharma is like the light of the sun illuminating the four continents; wherever it travels, it is able to dispel the darkness.
Why is this? Because the nature of the sun is inherently luminous, it is thus able to illuminate all things.
"The Upādhyāya is likewise so now; because he has practiced from the beginning, his wisdom is clear and lucid, and with this luminous wisdom, he dispels the darkness of sentient beings.
When the Lord of Devas had spoken these words, eighty thousand devas all rose together, adjusted their robes, paid homage, knelt with palms joined, and said to the jackal:

"We pray that the Honored One will take pity on us and bestow upon us the ten wholesome dharmas, which will bring great benefit, profit, and peace to sentient beings, and also cause the merits of our Upādhyāya to increase further."
He replied, "Excellent; you should know that now is the time.
He then addressed Śakra, Lord of Devas, saying:
Regarding the method for receiving the precepts, one must first perform repentance to purify the body, speech, and mind.
What is meant by physical karma?
It consists of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
What is called verbal action?
False speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech.
What is called mental action?
Envy, malice, pride, and false views—these constitute the ten [unwholesome] things.
To restrain the actions of body, speech, and mind, and not to commit various evils, is called the ten wholesome deeds.
To act unrestrainedly with body, speech, and mind, creating various evil karmas, is called the ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśala*).

To single-mindedly and sincerely repent and eliminate these ten unwholesome actions—because the ten unwholesome actions are extinguished, body, speech, and mind become pure; because the three karmas are pure, it is called the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*).
The Heavenly Lord asked,
"What is the retribution for the merit of the ten wholesome actions? The jackal replied:

"I have heard the Buddha say that if a person practices the ten wholesome deeds, the karmic retribution for those ten wholesome deeds will lead to rebirth in the six heavens of the desire realm, where there are palaces made of the seven treasures, the five desires arise spontaneously, food and drink of a hundred flavors are provided, and one's lifespan is immeasurable; moreover, one's parents, wife, children, and six types of relatives will all be upright, pure, and clean, living in joy and happiness."

If those among the various devas who maintain the ten wholesome paths exhaust their heavenly merit and are reborn again within the heavens, their karmic rewards will become even more excellent, differing from the retribution for the ten wholesome paths experienced by worldly people.
Why is this so? When worldly people cultivate goodness, the three precepts of the path of mind are difficult to maintain and uphold.
Regarding the precept of non-anger, one must first employ skillful means to practice a mind of loving-kindness; only then can the precept of non-anger be accomplished.
The compassion practiced by worldly people is difficult to sustain for long; it is like water being cut by a blade, which breaks apart as soon as it is struck but immediately recombines.
Holding the precept of non-anger is likewise so.
As for the precept against jealousy, its manifestation occurs at specific times.
What is the occasion?

It is when one sees another obtain profit, see another enjoy pleasure, see another possess physical beauty, see another be courageous and strong, see another be intelligent, or see another cultivate merit—in short, upon seeing any such superior matter, it is at that time that envy arises in one's mind.
Therefore, you should know that the mind of envy arises at certain times. The mind of arrogance also arises at certain times:

when one sees a foolish person, the mind of arrogance arises; when one sees an ugly person, an impure person, or a poor person—to speak briefly—when one sees those who are deaf, blind, lame, or crippled, those with deficient faculties, or those of the Yi, Man, Hu, and Lu tribes, the mind of arrogance arises only upon seeing them.
Therefore, one should know that the precept against arrogance is occasioned by specific circumstances.
For this reason, the mental precept of worldly people is difficult to maintain; even if they strive to uphold it, they occasionally attain it and occasionally forget it.

Therefore, although worldly people receive celestial blessings as the karmic retribution for the ten wholesome deeds, they do not equal the merit of the ten wholesome deeds of the devas; in terms of radiance, supernatural power, sustenance, and the marks of excellence, the latter are preeminent and supreme.
This is likewise true regarding their knowledge of past lives.
"Therefore, you should know that the karmic rewards for gods and humans who practice the ten wholesome paths of action surpass those of worldly people.
The Heavenly Lord said:

"As the Venerable One has explained, when people practice the ten wholesome paths, it is difficult to maintain the three precepts of the mind; it is the same for gods and humans. Jealousy, anger, arrogance, and false views—such mental states as these are never absent. How then can their meritorious rewards surpass those of worldly people?"
The jackal replied:
"Although such heavenly beings exist, they are not like those of the human world. Why is this so?"
The devas and humans possess merit and virtue; their suffering is slight and their joy is abundant, and their afflictions weigh lightly upon their minds.
Worldly people possess meager merit; their joy is slight and their suffering is abundant, and their afflictions weigh heavily upon their minds.
The Lord of Devas replied:

"Since time immemorial, the gods have been accustomed to pleasure and their minds are coarse, much like monkeys; though they now uphold the ten wholesome virtues, they may later neglect and forget them."
"When one has committed a transgression,
what should be done? The jackal replied,

"I have heard the Teacher say that if a person who practices the ten wholesome deeds should commit a lapse and perform unwholesome acts, they ought to go before a wise and meritorious person, confess and repent for whatever offense was committed, and receive the precepts once again from them."
A practitioner who acts in this way does not lose their precepts. Why is this?

The ten wholesome precepts are like grain seedlings, while afflictions are like weeds. Weeds and the upright seedlings mutually obstruct one another; therefore, in order for the seedlings to grow, one must remove the weeds and impurities. Because the grain seedlings are pure, the harvest will surely be abundant. Because the grain is plentiful, there will ultimately be no hunger or want.

At that time, when the Lord of the Devas and eighty thousand devas heard these matters, they were filled with great joy. No longer worrying about the exhaustion of merit, impermanence, or the retribution of the evil realms, they humbly reflected to themselves:

"Although the practice of wholesome merit brings no bitter retribution, there is still birth and death from which one cannot escape impermanence. Furthermore, the King of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations, seeing people cultivate merit, harbors jealousy and creates obstacles; he causes them to forget the path of goodness and leads them to commit evil deeds. Due to the causes and conditions of such evil karma, one ought to undergo bitter retribution."
He said to the jackal,
"By cultivating what merit can one always remain undying and not be deluded or disturbed by the King of Māras?
The jackal replied:

"I have heard the Master teach that one who resolves to attain Bodhicitta and cultivates the deeds of a Bodhisattva cannot be thwarted by Māra Pāpīyān, because their mind is not deluded. Wherever they are born, their wisdom is clear and lucid; because their wisdom is clear and lucid, they constantly remember their past lives; because they remember their past lives, they do not give rise to evil karma; because their minds are pure, they attain the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); and because they possess this patience of non-arising, they do not regress from the Path, remaining far removed from the sorrows, afflictions, and sufferings of birth and death."
The Heavenly King asked:
"In practicing the path of a bodhisattva, what dharmas should one cultivate?
The jackal replied:

"I have heard the Master say that those who seek the Buddha-way begin from the origin; first, they should extensively study the causes and conditions of all phenomena. Because they understand causes and conditions, their faith becomes firm and solid. By the power of the faculty of faith, they are able to give rise to diligence. By the power of diligence, they do not give rise to the causes and conditions of any unwholesome karma. Because their purely wholesome mind is free from negligence, wisdom is perfected. By the power of wisdom, they comprehensively encompass all thirty-seven factors of enlightenment that assist the path to Bodhi."
The Heavenly Emperor asked:

"As Your Reverence has taught, the meaning of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is vast and profound; it cannot be fully understood by one with a coarse mind in a sudden moment. How, then, can one enter the practice of the Bodhisattva path?"
The jackal replied:
“I have heard your teacher say that one who cultivates the path of a bodhisattva first tames the sense faculties through skillful means (*upāya*).
What, then, are these skillful means?”
"It refers to the six pāramitās and the four immeasurable minds; these are called the skillful means for subduing the sense faculties.
The Lord of Devas asked:
"What is the meaning of the six pāramitās?"
"I only pray that you will explain this. The jackal replied,
"The foremost form of giving is the breaking of the mind of stinginess and greed, because one has no lingering regret."
Second, guarding the good by not committing evil;
third, being able to endure encountering adverse circumstances with a mind free from the intent to retaliate;
fourth, diligently practicing the path and its tasks without slackening or retreating.
Fifth is to collect and restrain the mind so that it does not engage in improper thoughts.
Sixth is to cultivate wisdom in order to illuminate and eliminate the darkness of afflictions and ignorance.
These are what are called the six pāramitās.
Through the power of skillful means in the six pāramitās, one subdues the sense faculties.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which the sense faculties are subdued. What are these four?
First is the mind of loving-kindness, second is the mind of compassion, third is the mind of sympathetic joy, and fourth is the mind of equanimity.
These four matters are called the immeasurable minds.
The Heavenly Lord asked:
"How does one practice loving-kindness?
The jackal replied:
"When seeing those in distress and hardship, one should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and act as their protector, ensuring that all find their proper place.
What is meant by compassion (*karuṇā*)?

Seeing that all sentient beings, due to ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), create the karma of birth and death and undergo suffering in the five realms of existence without being able to escape it on their own—therefore, I should not now be indolent, but should instead diligently apply myself with vigor to cultivate wisdom and swiftly attain the Buddha-way. Having attained the Buddha-way, I shall use the light of wisdom to illuminate and dispel the dark gloom of ignorance for sentient beings, enabling them to see the Great Radiance and be freed from the bonds of manifold sufferings."

Although I have not yet attained Buddhahood, whatever virtuous deeds I perform in all my activities, I dedicate them to sentient beings so that they may obtain peace and happiness; if sentient beings have transgressions, I shall take them upon myself in their stead.
This is called compassion.
What is meant by sympathetic joy?
It is when one sees worldly people practicing wholesome deeds and seeking the fruits of the three vehicles, and one encourages, assists, and rejoices in them.
Seeing those who experience happiness, their hearts likewise rejoice;

seeing those who are upright, those who are brave and strong, those who are wealthy and noble, those who possess wisdom, those with a compassionate heart, and those who are filial and obedient—in short, they encourage, assist, and rejoice in all virtuous people.
This is the mind of joy.
What is meant by equanimity?

It refers to all meritorious deeds performed through giving; bestowing kindness upon others without hoping for reward in the present life, without hoping for reward in a future rebirth, and without hoping for reward in subsequent lives.
This is called equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Accomplishing these four matters is termed the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa-citta*).
Because sentient beings are immeasurable, the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is immeasurable; [and so forth for the other three].
Because sentient beings are immeasurable, compassion is also immeasurable;
because sentient beings are immeasurable, sympathetic joy is also immeasurable;
because sentient beings are immeasurable, equanimity is also immeasurable.
Therefore, these are called the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).
Together with the preceding six perfections, they are termed the ten pāramitās.
These ten pāramitās comprehensively encompass all the practices of the bodhisattva path.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, having heard the jackal explain the causes and conditions for the merit of practicing the ten wholesome paths of action, and further having heard the meaning and intent of the causes and conditions for a bodhisattva’s practice of the path to enlightenment, the net of his doubts was severed. Joy and exultation pervaded his entire body, and he immediately rose with his eighty thousand attendant devas to pay further respect. With palms joined, he addressed the jackal, saying:
"Today, my disciples—the eighty thousand devas—have simultaneously and with one mind resolved to attain bodhicitta."
"As the Upādhyāya has taught regarding the practice of the Bodhisattva path, I shall fully and reverently carry it out.
I only pray that the Upādhyāya will graciously grant his approval and consent. The jackal replied:
"You should know that this is the time; this is precisely what your original heart desired.
Thereupon, Śakra, Lord of Devas, said to the jackal, "Venerable One, what is the ritual for your food and drink?"
"I only pray that you will instruct me on how I should prepare an offering. The jackal replied,
"The manner of his eating is not fit for human ears to hear."

Why is this? Due to the causes and conditions of their sinful karma, the food they consume is utterly impure; their forms resemble those of animals and are no different from those of hungry ghosts. Fortunately, there is no need to inquire about the food they eat.
The Heavenly King said:

"Venerable Upādhyāya, whether your food and drink are good, you should let me know; or if they are poor, you should tell me. Your disciple shall now provide offerings according to what is appropriate."

The jackal replied, “I constantly eat the excrement and urine of lions, tigers, and wolves, as well as the skeletal remains of the dead and tattered clothes and hides found among burial mounds; however, if I am unable to obtain such food and am driven by the pangs of hunger and poverty, I will even eat earth and clay.”
"As for the retribution of the fruits of sin and suffering, from birth until death, though we eat impure things, we have never been satisfied.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the assembly of devas, having heard the jackal describe the nature of food and drink, were moved with sorrow and grief; their hearts pained by weeping, they said to the jackal:
"We disciples now wish to provide offerings, yet as you have said, our wishes will not be fulfilled. What can be done?"
"Now that we are returning to our celestial palaces, what means should we employ to repay the profound kindness of our teacher? The jackal replied:

"If you all now hear the Dharma from me and, upon returning to the heavens, successively teach and awaken the various devas—whether male or female—even if it be but a single person who is led to believe, accept, and practice it, this will not only repay my kindness but also repay the kindness of all Buddhas. As you teach and transform others, you will naturally increase your own merit and virtue as devas; how much more so if you teach and awaken many people, for the karmic reward would be immeasurable."
The devas rose and said to the jackal, "We, your disciples, are now returning to our celestial palaces.
We do not know, Venerable Sir, when you shall cast off this body reaping the retribution of sin and be born in heaven so that we may see one another."
The jackal replied, "When seven days have passed, I shall cast off this sinful body and be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven; you all may likewise aspire to be born in that heaven."
"Why is this? Because within Tuṣita Heaven there are many bodhisattvas who preach the Dharma and provide instruction for the sake of all devas and humans seeking the path to Buddhahood.
The Heavenly Lord replied:

"As instructed by your reverence, when the disciples and their retinue have exhausted their merit in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and their lives have ended, they shall all be reborn in that Tuṣita Heaven, where they may meet their teacher and uphold his instructions, just as we have vowed."
Having spoken these words, he scattered celestial flowers and incense upon the jackal and then departed.

After the devas had gone, the jackal did not leave its original seat; with single-minded devotion, it focused its thoughts exclusively on the ten dharmas of wholesome conduct and no longer went out to seek food.

After his life ended seven days later, he was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven as a prince among the devas; he again remembered his past lives and further taught the ten wholesome paths of action to the devas.
The Buddha said to the king:
"The jackal at that time was none other than myself."
The Lord Śakra, King of Devas at that time, was Śāriputra.
The great teacher Upatiṣya who instructed Ajita at that time was Maitreya.
The eighty thousand devas were the eighty thousand non-retrogressive bodhisattvas currently in this Sahā world-system.
The Buddha said, “Great King!

Recall the past, from the time I first resolved to attain enlightenment and practiced the bodhisattva path until the stage of non-arising. During that interval, for the sake of seeking the Dharma, I constantly exerted diligent effort alongside Maitreya, Śāriputra, and others. Disregarding my own body and life, I pursued enlightened teachers, attending upon them with devotion, refining my studies, and perfecting wisdom.”
By the power of wisdom, wherever they are born within the five realms of existence, they teach and bring to maturity immeasurable sentient beings, enabling them to transcend suffering.

Up until their attainment of Buddhahood, it is entirely through the skillful means of Prajñā-wisdom that they sever all latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) and causal conditions, thereby achieving Equal and Perfect Enlightenment.
Furthermore, by means of wisdom, one teaches and transforms sentient beings within the Sahā world-system, delivering them from the sufferings of the three realms of existence.
For this reason, I say that the wisdom of *prajñā* has four names and meanings.

At that time, King Prasenajit and his retinue, having heard what the Buddha had said, found their minds opened and liberated. Rising again, they prostrated themselves, leaping for joy with exultation. Standing with palms joined, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Having now come to see the Buddha, we have swiftly attained a great and wholesome benefit; we listen to the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma without knowing fatigue or weariness. Why is this so?

Previously, when the World-Honored One spoke of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination—the supramundane path—our faculties were dull and we were bewildered and unable to understand; because we did not understand, our bodies became weary and exhausted.

Now that I have heard the Buddha’s exposition of the bodhisattva practices, although I do not yet fully understand them, my heart feels profound love and joy; I thirst for and long to hear them, with no sense of satiety.

Your disciple now wishes to resolve upon the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) and seek the unsurpassed path. I only pray that the World-Honored One will, out of compassion, grant me permission and instruct me in the rules and methods of bodhisattva conduct, so that I may practice exactly as taught.
The Buddha said to the king:

“As for the practice of the Dharma by a Bodhisattva, as described above—namely, the ten paths of wholesome action through the deeds of body, speech, and mind, and the ten pāramitās which comprehensively encompass all dharmas that assist the path to Buddhahood—are you able to practice these?”
The King said:
“As the World-Honored One has taught regarding the ten courses of wholesome action, three among them pertain to the mental path and are difficult to maintain.
How should they be received so that they are not lost or leaked away?”
The Buddha told the king:

"The minds of worldly people are coarse, like those of monkeys; they are tossed and turned by the winds of various afflictions. Therefore, one who wishes to practice the ten paths of wholesome action must not delay; one who wishes to cultivate the ten wholesome actions should limit them to three periods of the day."
What are the three periods?
From dawn until the time for the morning meal is called the first period;
the duration of one meal is called the middle period; [the remainder of the day is the last period].
When walking a hundred paces, it is called the "lower" stage.

Receiving the ten wholesome dharmas according to one's capacity, one guards the mind during that time, firmly upholding the three precepts so that they are not lost; this is what is meant by practicing the ten wholesome deeds.
The King said:
"If, as the World-Honored One has taught, the merit of one who observes the ten wholesome actions for only three periods of time is exceedingly slight, how can such a person generate blessings?
The Buddha told the King:
"When a person cultivates the ten wholesome paths of action, although the duration may be brief, the merit and retribution are exceedingly vast. Why is this?
Because the three precepts of the mental path are difficult to guard; thus, even if they are observed for only a short time, the resulting retribution is immeasurable."
For example, suppose someone were to gather wood and grass over the course of a hundred years and burn them with fire; they would be consumed and extinguished in an instant.
Therefore, one should know that practicing even a small amount of goodness for a short time can extinguish immeasurable evil karma and grave offenses.

Furthermore, it is like drilling for fire: by applying diligent effort, one obtains fire in an instant; the power of that fire can burn all the grasses, trees, and forests under heaven until they are exhausted, at which point it finally ceases.

Great King, you should know that it is likewise for a person who cultivates the ten wholesome actions: even for a mere moment, such power can extinguish immeasurable evil karma and grave offenses; it can cause the sprout of Bodhi to arise in the practitioner, and as that sprout develops, it gradually grows until the fruit of Buddhahood is attained.
Having heard this, the king rose again and paid homage; filled with great joy and celebrating what he had never before experienced, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I, your disciple, have now attained a great and wholesome benefit."

Why is this? Having heard the World-Honored One’s teaching that the causal conditions of the merit of practicing the ten paths of wholesome action can cause sentient beings to produce the sprout of Bodhi, we disciples now aspire to Bodhi; we shall diligently practice it with minds that do not retreat.

When the Buddha had spoken these words, more than five thousand people—including the king’s retinue of ministers and officials, the palace ladies, the fourfold assembly of disciples, devas, nāgas, spirits, humans, and non-humans—vowed to attain the mind of unsurpassed bodhicitta.

At that time, the chief queen of King Prasenajit always employed four men for her comings and goings. Their name was Śāṇḍilī; "Śāṇḍilī" in the language of Han means "stone-woman. Because she lacked the sexual organs of male or female, she was called a stone-woman. She possessed the greatest physical strength, and these four men were made to carry the queen’s palanquin.
The queen’s palanquin made of the seven treasures was left outside the gate of the Jetavana Monastery, and she commanded the eunuchs to guard it.
The eunuchs, in turn, ordered Caturmahārājika to guard the lady’s carriage, while he himself went to the Buddha’s side to listen to the Dharma.
Śāṇḍilī and the others were sleeping beneath their palanquins and were unaware.
At that time, a wicked man stole a *maṇi* jewel from the precious palanquin of the lady.
At that time, the eunuch briefly went out to inspect the palanquin; not seeing the precious jewel, his heart was filled with terror. Fearing the lady’s reprimand, he asked the stone woman:
"I sent you to guard the palanquin; why did you steal the jewel?"
Each of them replied, "We truly did not steal.
The eunuch was greatly enraged; he whipped the stone woman until her agony pierced to the very bone.

At that time, there was a stone woman who, realizing she had not stolen anything and yet was being subjected to cruel torture, fled in haste and broke into the vihāra, crying out in grievance with loud lamentations; the entire assembly heard her but did not know its cause.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"You may go out to where that eunuch is; do not allow him to whip an innocent person who has committed no transgression.
For what reason?..."

These four stone women were, in fact, the Queen’s teachers in a previous life; since they themselves were without fault or transgression, why did you strike them with whips so recklessly, thereby creating the causes and conditions for evil karma in future lives?
At that time, having heard these words of the Buddha, the Queen immediately rose with reverence, joined her palms, and addressed the Buddha:
"As the World-Honored One has said, the woman who bore no children and carried the four stone burdens was indeed my preceptor in a previous life."
The assembly was bewildered and did not understand; they only wished that the World-Honored One would explain the causes and conditions so that all those gathered might hear and know them.
The Buddha told the Queen:
"Summon the barren woman and test her truthfulness before the World-Honored One."
The Queen, having received the command, immediately dispatched a eunuch to seize her and bring her back.

At that time, the four stone-maidens saw the Buddha; they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and wept, then knelt for a long time with palms joined and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"We truly did not steal the jewels. For what reason have we been falsely implicated in this crime? We have been whipped until our bodies are broken by the agonizing pain."
The World-Honored One replied:
"The causes and conditions of sinful karma are created by oneself; they are not wrought by one's parents, nor do they fall from the heavens.
When a person performs good or evil deeds, they receive the retribution of suffering or joy, just as an echo responds to a sound."
Greedy for immediate profit, one’s mind acts with deceit and flattery, unaware that in future lives one will suffer calamities for many kalpas.
Indeed, evil originates from the mind and turns back to harm oneself, just as rust produced by iron consumes and destroys its own form.
The king joined his palms and addressed the Buddha:
“In all the teachings you have given previously, there were always causes and conditions. Now, regarding these four stone women, what were the causes and conditions for their origins in past lives?”
"I pray that the Buddha will explain this for me, so as to enlighten those who are blind and ignorant, bringing great benefit and blessing to all people.
The Buddha told the king:
"It is well that you wish to hear it; fix your mind and listen attentively, for I shall now speak of it."
