Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Tanying of the Xiao Qi Dynasty.
The Buddha again reflected: "Now within my Dharma there are bhikṣus whose words and deeds do not accord and whose minds and mouths are at variance.

Some act for the sake of gain, wealth, food, and drink; some for the sake of reputation or to gather a circle of followers; others have left home to practice the Way out of a distaste for royal laws and corvée labor. None of them possess the mind directed toward the three gates of liberation to cross over the suffering of the three realms of existence."
Because they receive offerings from the faithful with impure minds, unaware that in future lives they will suffer calamities for kalpas to repay their past debts;
for the sake of such people, how could one not speak?
The Buddha told the king:

"Recall that in the past, incalculable kalpas ago, there was a great kingdom named Vaiśālī. In it lived a woman named Devadattā, of Brahmin descent; her husband had died and she remained a widow. Her family was immensely wealthy, yet she had no children and no parents; left alone and destitute, she had no one to rely upon."
According to the Dharma of the Brahmins, if things do not go as desired, they will give rise to the practice of self-immolation.
From time to time, various Brahmins would go together to the place where Devadatta was and instruct him, saying:
"The misfortunes of your present life are all caused by the transgressions of your previous lives."
What is meant by "sin"?
It is failing to respectfully serve and honor the various Brahmins; furthermore, being unfilial toward one's parents and husband, and lacking a compassionate heart in raising one's children.
Because of these sins, one is caused to experience loneliness and endure misfortune in this present life.
"If you do not now cultivate merit and extinguish your sins, in future lives they will become even more severe as you fall into hell; at that time, it will be too late for regret.
Tiwei asked, "What kind of merit should one perform to extinguish one's sins?"
The Brahmin said: "There are two ways to extinguish sin.

For a light offense, one should shave one's own head with one's own hands, bathe in fragrant water, enter a temple, repent and offer apologies to the god Nārāyaṇa, and invite at least one hundred Brahmins to provide them with food and drink."

Having provided the food and drink, he should give a hundred milch cows with their calves as a religious gift (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahmins; only then will his transgression be extinguished. Why is this?

Because the Brahmins practice the pure Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*), abstaining from wine, meat, and the five pungent herbs—scallions, garlic, and the like—and rely solely on cow’s milk for their sustenance. This causes the donor and patron to extinguish their transgressions and generate merit, so that in every life they are born into and their wishes are fulfilled according to their hearts.
Your present transgression is grave; you ought to give all the precious treasures and possessions within your home as alms to five hundred great brahmins.
Once these brahmins have received the offerings, they shall perform incantations and prayers on your behalf, so that in future lives you may always attain great wealth.

Those who wish to extinguish their transgressions should pile wood by the banks of the Ganges and burn themselves. Then the brahmins shall offer prayers and benedictions, so that all light and heavy offenses committed in previous lives may be extinguished at once; in future lives, they shall be reborn without further calamity, and their parents, brothers, husbands, and children shall enjoy immeasurable life and infinite happiness.
Thereupon, Tīva gave his consent; with a resolute mind, he decided to burn himself alive.
He then commanded his servants to take ten wagons into the mountains to gather firewood, intending to use it for his self-immolation.

"At that time, there was a practitioner in the kingdom named Patipā, which in the local language means 'Eloquent. He was diligent in observing the precepts, possessed great learning and wisdom, and constantly used a heart of compassion to transform the world, leading people to abandon error for the right, cast aside evil, and cultivate goodness."
It was reported that Tiwei intended to burn his own body; moved by compassion, [the Buddha] went to where he was and asked Tiwei:
"Having prepared the wood and fire, what do you intend to do?"
Devadatta replied,
"I wish to burn my own body to eliminate my calamities and sins. Prajñākūṭa answered:
"Karmic offenses from previous lives follow the spirit and do not merge with the body; how could merely suffering by burning the body possibly extinguish those offenses?

For humans, fortune and misfortune arise in accordance with the mind: because the mind contemplates good, one receives a good retribution; because the mind contemplates evil, one receives an evil retribution; and it is the same for the retribution of suffering and pleasure when the mind contemplates them."

Just as one who dies of hunger becomes a hungry ghost (*preta*), one who dies in suffering receives the retribution of suffering, one who dies in joy receives the retribution of joy, and for those who die in peace and happiness, the fruit of their retribution is likewise so.
"How can you, in the midst of such suffering and affliction, seek to extinguish your sins and hope for a favorable retribution?
You ought not to do so; it is logically inconsistent.
"Furthermore, Devadatta, it is like a person who is gravely ill and oppressed by pain. If a wicked person were to come to him, revile and scold the patient, and strike his ears with his hand."
"What do you think?
At that time, would that sick person have a virtuous mind, free from anger and resentment? Tiwei replied:
“That man is afflicted by illness; even before meeting anyone, he constantly harbors resentment and vexation—how much more so when his ears are seized?
How could he possibly remain without anger? Prajñākūṭa said:

“If you are now like this because of the sins of your previous lives, guarding poverty and embracing calamity while constantly harboring sorrow and vexation, and yet wish to burn your body to escape that sorrow and vexation—can you truly achieve it?”
Suppose a person who is already afflicted by illness were to be scolded and reviled by another; their suffering would increase a hundred thousand million times over.

How much more so when one burns one's own body? When the fierce flames arise, the body is scorched and rotted away; yet because the breath has not ceased and the mind has not perished, at that moment the body and mind are being boiled while consciousness has not yet departed. Consequently, one suffers from poisonous torment and mental anguish. Upon dying from this state, one is reborn in hell, where the suffering and affliction become even more intense, increasing a hundred thousand million times over. It is extremely difficult to seek escape from such a fate, let alone desire to burn the body as a means to leave suffering behind.
Furthermore, Devadatta!

It is like an ox that, weary of its cart, wishes for the cart to be destroyed; yet even if the front cart is destroyed, it immediately encounters a subsequent cart that yokes its neck, for its transgressions have not yet been exhausted.

Human beings are also like this: even if one were to burn away hundreds of thousands of millions of bodies, the continuity of the causes and conditions of one’s sinful karma would not be extinguished.

It is like in the Avīci Hell, where all the sinners are burned; within a single day they die eighty thousand times and are reborn eighty thousand times, and only after the passing of an entire kalpa does their retribution finally come to an end.
"How much less so now, when you have burned your body only once in an attempt to seek the extinction of your sins; how could there be any principle by which this would be achieved?

At that time, the Eloquence (Pratibhāna) expounded the True Dharma through various causes and conditions. The mind of the woman Devadattā opened and her thoughts were liberated; she changed her resolve and altered her conduct, ceasing her intention to burn her body, and said to the Eloquence:
"What intention should I adopt to ensure the extinction of my sins?"
Pratibhāna replied:
"The evil committed by the former mind is like clouds obscuring the moon; the goodness arising from the latter mind is like a torch dispelling darkness.

Since you now fortunately possess the intent to extinguish your transgressions, there is a skillful means available: I can cause you to eliminate your calamities and sins without spending a single coin, nor even undergoing a fraction of suffering, so that you may enjoy peace and security in this life, and in future births, your virtuous aspirations shall be fulfilled according to your heart's desire."

Upon hearing this, Tiwei was filled with great joy; his grief and fear were instantly dispelled, like a prisoner of heavy crime who has received a pardon and is about to be released. He immediately rose to pay his respects, prostrating and inquiring after her well-being. He then commanded his servants to prepare a high seat, adorned to the utmost with *karpāsa* wool, fine woolen rugs, brocades, and embroidered hangings. Scattering flowers and burning incense, he entreated the eloquent lady to ascend the high seat.
Having accepted the invitation, Biancai ascended the high seat.

The woman Tiwei then led her household slaves, servants, and kinsmen—some five hundred people in all—to surround Biancai; they prostrated themselves with reverence, joined their palms, and stood before him.
The woman Devī addressed Prajñāpāramitā, saying:
"Regarding the causes for the eradication of sin that you have just explained, although I harbor great joy, I still have a slight doubt."
"I only pray that you will explain for me the method for removing transgressions, so that I may practice according to the Dharma.
Pratibhāna replied, "The causes from which transgressions arise are the body, speech, and mind. Unwholesome bodily karma consists of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct;..."
Unwholesome actions of speech—false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech;
unwholesome actions of mind—envy, malice, arrogance, and wrong views:
these constitute the ten unwholesome paths of action, which result in evil retributions.

Now, with single-minded sincerity, I shall repent; whatever such offenses I have committed in the past or in this present life, I now repent of them all, so as to bring forth these transgressions and extinguish them.
I shall now make this vow: from this day forward, I dare not commit such transgressions again.
Furthermore, for all the faults and offenses of our deceased ancestors, parents, husbands, and brothers, I now single-mindedly repent on their behalf.

My disciple Devadatta, through the causal conditions of merit from his present repentance, reforming evil, and practicing good, bestows these upon all sentient beings who suffer, so that they may obtain happiness.
"May I take upon myself the transgressions of all sentient beings.

Furthermore, I make this vow: by virtue of my turning away from evil today to follow the right path, repenting my sins, and cultivating merit, may I, throughout the succession of bodies from this life until the attainment of Buddhahood, always encounter enlightened teachers and meet virtuous friends. May my lifespan be immeasurable, and may I always be protected by my parents, husband, children, and six kinds of relatives, never undergoing suffering or affliction as I do now."
Thereupon, Pratibhāna said to Devadatta,
"The method for repenting transgressions and extinguishing sins is entirely like this.
Then Devadatta and his retinue knelt before Pratibhāna with palms joined and addressed him, saying:

"Your disciple has followed your venerable instructions and performed the repentance according to the Dharma. We pray that you would further bestow upon us teachings of other wholesome dharmas; we shall diligently practice them to increase our original merit."
Prajñākūṭa said: "Now you should sincerely take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus; recite this three times.
Now you should undertake the ten paths of wholesome action for as long as you live."
"I, disciple [Name], from this time forth for as long as life lasts, shall not kill, shall not steal, and shall not engage in sexual misconduct; these are the wholesome karmas of the body.
I shall not speak falsely, nor use double-tongued speech, nor speak harshly, nor engage in frivolous chatter; these are the wholesome karmas of speech.
I shall not harbor envy, anger, arrogance, or wrong views; these are the wholesome karmas of the mind."
"This is what is called the Dharma of the Ten Wholesome Precepts.
At that time, after Pratibhāna had instructed Devadatta in the ten wholesome dharmas, Devadatta’s retinue rejoiced and leaped for joy, and they practiced them with all their hearts.
He prepared various foods of a hundred flavors and diverse precious jewels for the woman Devī, then knelt on his right knee with palms joined and addressed Prajñāpāramitā, saying:
"I pray that you, O Honored One, will deign to remain and compassionately instruct me."
"Now we shall build a palace for you, Master; wherever it may be convenient, we shall serve you for the rest of our lives.
Prajñākūṭa replied, "Since you have now been able to abandon the heterodox and follow the orthodox, purifying yourself through the ten wholesome deeds, you are true sons of the Dharma."
Furthermore, by teaching the ten wholesome deeds to transform the world, you will have repaid the profound kindness of your teachers and companions.
You have already attained deliverance; it is not fitting for me to remain.
I shall now go to transform other regions.

At that time, Devadatta, knowing that his teacher would not remain, transported the various treasures and precious objects from the storehouse to present them to his teacher, hoping that he might take them to heart.
Vāgīśa did not accept them; he took his leave and departed.
Thereupon, Devadatta thought to himself:
"That I have been saved this day is entirely due to my honored teacher and preceptor’s enlightenment and accomplishment.
His profound kindness in instructing me has reached its limit; he has refused my earnest entreaties to remain and will not accept even precious treasures. What should I do?"
Filled with grief and sorrow, her tears flowed freely as she prostrated herself in thanks and took her leave.
After Biancai had departed, the woman Tiwei and her retinue of over five hundred people constantly transformed one another through the ten wholesome dharmas for a long period of time.
At that time, a famine suddenly befell the kingdom, and the people suffered from hunger.

There were five bhikṣus who were indolent and remiss; they did not cultivate their studies of the scriptures or their understanding of their principles, nor did they single-mindedly practice the precepts with diligence. Consequently, the people of the world looked down upon them and failed to provide for them; they fell into poverty and distress, having no further means of livelihood.
The five men deliberated, saying:
"In the affairs of human life, one must act according to the exigencies of the moment. Human life is of the utmost importance; why should we cling to death?

Together they went begging for alms and prepared a rope bed in the wilderness. They swept the ground until it was clean and adorned it with flowers and banners. Seated in order, their outward appearance resembled that of practitioners in meditative trance, yet within they harbored depraved and turbid thoughts.

When the people of the world saw him, they declared him to be a sage; they brought and offered him a hundred kinds of food and drink, gathering like clouds to provide for him, so that the five men were fully satiated with more than enough.
At that time, having heard of this matter, Devadatta dispatched men to search for them. The messengers returned and reported:
"There are five holy men sitting alone in the mountain marshes; people from all quarters gather there like clouds, as if worshipping celestial deities."
Devadatta was filled with joy and congratulated himself,
saying, "My wish has been fulfilled. At dawn,
he immediately ordered his precious chariot to be prepared with incense, flowers, and music, and went to the five bhikṣus.
When Devadatta had arrived, he paid homage, inquired after his well-being, and provided offerings.
When the meal was finished, Devadatta and his retinue joined their palms in reverence and addressed the bhikṣu, saying:
"Your venerable virtue is most weighty; you are the unsurpassed field of merit. Sentient beings receive your blessings."
One should not disparage oneself.
It is my humble wish as a disciple to invite your venerable spirit to grace my poor dwelling and allow me to manifest my sincere devotion.
I only pray that you will look upon us with compassion and pity, delivering all living beings.
Your disciple also possesses a pure garden, with flowing springs and bathing pools, magnificently adorned and radiant.
"Thus, as Ajātaśatru and his retinue prostrated themselves again and again, the five bhikṣus, perceiving the sincerity of his intent, granted their consent. Ajātaśatru was filled with joy;
he took his leave and returned home, whereupon he immediately dispatched messengers to prepare a magnificent jeweled chariot to go and welcome the five bhikṣus back to his house for offerings."

The woman Tiwei possessed a beautiful garden not far from her house; it was ten *qǐng* in length and breadth, filled with flowing springs and bathing pools, various rare flowers and fruits, and *xiāoqīng* ducks and mandarin ducks—pure, magnificent, and exquisite.
Within that garden, he constructed a hall adorned with various jewels.
Inside the hall, he arranged couches, mats, and many exquisite bedding materials of the highest fragrance and purity, and had the five bhikṣus dwell therein.

The woman Tiwei served him for the rest of her life, attending to his every need according to the season; she provided food, drink, and medicinal decoctions, and carried out his commands without missing a single appointed time.
At that time, the five bhikṣus, having received such generous and abundant hospitality from their host, lived in peace and happiness, and they congratulated themselves, saying:
"How has this come about so suddenly?"

Now, when people are born into this world, they employ various means to seek wealth and profit in order to relieve their poverty; yet even if they achieve their desires, they do not compare to us, who enjoy fortune and emolument without exerting our bodies at all—is this not surely due to the power of wisdom?
The five bhikṣus observed that the host’s intentions were earnest and his hospitality profound; they deliberated together, saying:

"Although we have received from our host whatever provisions he can provide, his wealth is daily diminishing and his poverty will increase year by year, such that he cannot sustain us through the hardships of winter or enjoy prosperity and pleasure. We should now employ further skillful means to seek out wealth and riches, so that we may enjoy the pleasures of the five senses in the future."
Having made this deliberation, they took turns among themselves and dispatched one man to travel through various villages to proclaim to the people with these words:

"Those four bhikṣus dwell in seclusion and tranquility, upholding the prohibitive precepts; they have renounced wine and meat and do not eat onions or garlic. Their conduct accords with the Brahma-faring; they cultivate dhyāna and śamatha-vipaśyanā, and have realized untainted karma. Before long, through their practice, they will become arhats, serving as the unsurpassed field of merit for the world."
Having heard this, the multitude brought various kinds of wealth, money, food, and drink, gathering together to approach him with reverent offerings for many years.
The woman Tiwei, with a sincere heart of faith, made offerings as was appropriate, rejoicing without weariness.
When their lifespans ended and they passed away, they were reborn in the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations (*Nirmāṇarati*).

Those five bhikṣus, however, practiced craftiness and deceit; because of their wicked and turbid minds, when their merit was exhausted and their lives ended, they were reborn in hell, where they suffered great retributive suffering for eight thousand billion kalpas.
When their retribution in hell is exhausted, they take the form of hungry ghosts, *chi-mei*, or *wang-liang* spirits; thus they pass through successive states for eight thousand *kalpas*.

When their retribution as hungry ghosts is exhausted, they receive the bodies of six domestic animals to repay their former masters for the offerings received in previous lives. Through the causal conditions of karmic retribution, they may become camels, donkeys, mules, oxen, or horses, constantly repaying their masters with their physical strength wherever those masters enjoy the fruits of merit—thus they pass through another eight thousand lifetimes.

When her karmic retribution for the animal existence was completed, although she obtained a human body, her faculties were dull and obscured; she lacked both male and female sexual organs and was called a "stone-woman" (*śilā-strī*).
From that time until now, throughout eight thousand lifetimes, she has constantly repaid her master with her physical labor, and even now it does not cease.
The Buddha told the king:
"The one who was Devadatta at that time is the Queen.
The one who was Vāgīśa at that time is Maudgalyāyana."
"The five bhikṣus at that time were none other than the five people now following the Queen, including Śāntirā and the others who carried her palanquin.
The King addressed the Buddha, saying,
"As the World-Honored One has said, these five people gave rise to the cause;..."
"Now I see only four men carrying the litter; where is the other one?
The Buddha told the king, "The one person who is always inside the palace, who attends to the latrines and removes the excrement, is he."

Upon hearing this, the Queen was struck with solemn awe and her hair stood on end; filled with fear, she rose again to pay homage to the Buddha, and standing with palms joined, she addressed him, saying:

"If it is as the World-Honored One has said—that Śāṇḍila and the others were my teachers in previous lives—truly I am filled with anxiety and dread, fearing that I may have committed a crime of immediate retribution."

Why is this? For a person’s teacher, one ought to cultivate reverence; it is appropriate to bear them upon one's head and prostrate before them. Yet, you have instead made him carry a carriage and follow behind like an ox or a horse. Because of these causes and conditions, I feel profound fear.
"I pray that the Buddha will deign to show compassion and grant me leave to repent.
The Buddha told her, "The Queen’s merit and virtue are such that she has no faults or transgressions; why do you harbor fear and doubt?"
Sentient beings possess diverse natures and their karmic actions differ; the virtuous receive blessings, while the wicked naturally incur calamity.

When Your Majesty was in your former lives, you were straightforward in heart, pure, and with joyful faith you cultivated merit. By virtue of these causes and conditions of merit, from that time until now, in every birth you have successively encountered enlightened teachers, receiving and accepting their instructions and admonitions; thus you have proceeded from good to good and from fortune to fortune.
As for today, one naturally partakes of blessings and fortune, encountering the appearance of a Buddha in the world due to the power of the causes and conditions of merit from previous lives.
Furthermore, one hears the True Dharma and practices according to its teachings.
For these reasons, there is no fault or transgression.

As for the circumstances of the five Śreṇika brothers, because in their past lives they were wicked, turbid, and sycophantic, lacking any heart of compassion, they accepted your offerings; through the causal conditions of this karmic offense, they must now repay their former debts.
The Queen said: "Now that I have heard the Buddha’s discourse on the causes and conditions of one's past karma, my doubts as a disciple are resolved, and I no longer feel any anxiety or fear.
But as for this Śandhila, when will the retribution for her sinful karma ever come to an end?"
"Disciple, I have now released Śāṇḍilī; I dare not employ her as a servant, but allow her to go wherever she pleases.

I only pray that the World-Honored One will preach the Dharma to enlighten her, causing her mind to attain liberation, so that she may reform her evil ways, cultivate goodness, and swiftly escape from suffering."
The Buddha told him,
"If you wish for me to convert her now, summon that scavenger from within the palace.
The Queen immediately dispatched a messenger to call Śāṇḍilī.
The messenger received his orders and returned in a moment,
bringing Śāṇḍila and the other four men, who gathered together and stood before the Buddha.
Out of great compassion, the World-Honored One first comforted them with kind words, saying:
"O my sons, are you all in good health and spirits? Are you at peace and happy, free from suffering and distress?
The five men replied in anger, "The Buddha does not know the proper time."
Why is this? Day and night they toil with hardship, driven by whips and staffs, having no leisure for rest; what joy could there be in such a state?
How could the Buddha not know these matters, yet instead ask people whether they are happy or not?
The Buddha told the five men:

"The suffering of this present body all arises from the crookedness, deceit, and impurity of past lives; harboring unwholesome minds while receiving the offerings of others, such karmic causes and conditions have been produced through successive rebirths until reaching this present body. Even now, the karmic causes and conditions for repaying these offenses remain unfinished."
If you wish to seek liberation from the retribution of evil fruits, you should now, with a sincere and earnest heart, repent of your transgressions, reform your evils, and cultivate goodness;
through these causes and conditions, you may escape suffering.
When Śaṇḍila and the others heard the Buddha’s words, their anger flared up; they turned their backs toward the Buddha and refused to listen.
By means of his supernatural power, the Buddha caused a manifested Buddha to stand before them, using skillful means to console and exhort them to repent.
Śāntirā and the others again turned their faces toward the east;
once more, an emanation Buddha stood facing them.
They again turned toward the west, and yet another emanation Buddha appeared.
In the four intermediate directions, above, and below, there were Buddhas facing them in every direction.
When Śāntika and the others saw themselves surrounded by these Buddhas, the five men immediately cried out in grievance and lamentation, saying:
"We are now wretched and evil sinners; why does the Buddha now distress us so?"
At that time, the World-Honored One withdrew the manifested transformation-buddhas so as to become a single buddha-body.
The Buddha addressed the great assembly:
"O King, the Queen Mother, the bhikṣus, and others—do you see this Śrāmaṇera?"
They all replied, "So be it. [The Buddha said:
"You should know that the sinful karma of sentient beings involves two kinds of hindrances:
first, the hindrance of karma; second, the hindrance of afflictions."
Those with light offenses have the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*);

those with heavy offenses have the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*). Those such as the icchantikas possess both obstacles; because of their heavy karmic obstacles, they cannot be transformed and there is nothing that can be done for them.
At that time, the Queen, seeing that Śāṇḍila would not accept the Buddha’s transformation, was moved with deep sorrow and said to the five men:
"From this day forward, we shall forever sever our karmic ties; go wherever you please, east or west, free from anxiety and filled with joy."
Śāṇḍilī and the others knelt with their heads to the ground and, shedding tears, addressed the Queen, saying:
"We five women have served our mistress; what transgression have we committed that, against all expectation, we are today driven away and cast aside?"
"If there is anything that does not meet with your approval, we only pray for your great forbearance and that you allow us to serve as before.
Thereupon, the Queen declined their request repeatedly, yet Śāntirakṣita and the others were unwilling to depart.
The Queen said to the Buddha, "I have sincerely attempted to release Śāṇḍilī, but she is unwilling to leave;
what should I do? The Buddha told her:
“Śāṇḍila and the others have not yet finished repaying their debts; bound by the constraints of those causes and conditions, they cannot be released. There is nothing that can be done about this.
For now, let us comply with their wishes and restore their occupations; once the repayment of their karmic causes and conditions is complete, they shall naturally gain their freedom.”
The Buddha said to the king:
"When a person cultivates merit, practices humility and reverence, maintains a straightforward and pure mind, and engages in the work of the Path, their merit is immeasurable;
fire cannot burn them, water cannot sweep them away, thieves and robbers cannot find an opportunity against them, and even the powerful might of kings cannot move them."
Now the Empress enjoys celestial blessings.

Yet those who harbor evil intentions and crave immediate gain, such as Śveta, have suffered calamities through successive lifetimes that do not cease even now; though they encounter the transformation of the Sage, it passes by them like the wind over their ears. Due to the power of their sinful karma, they instead give rise to resentment and envy; dwelling in profound darkness and obscurity, when will they ever be delivered?
At that time, out of a heart of compassion, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"As I have previously said, it is difficult to obtain a human body; it is difficult to encounter a Buddha; it is difficult to hear the Dharma; and it is also difficult to live out one's full lifespan."

"You, my sons, by virtue of slight merit from previous lives, have been born into the human realm. Having encountered the Buddha while he was in the world, you heard the Dharma and received it with faith; you severed the bonds of affection and parted from your parents, brothers, wives, children, and six classes of kinsmen to leave the household life for the sake of the Way.

Like prisoners escaping from jail, you should abandon evil and follow good, ensuring that your inner thoughts correspond with your outward conduct and that your words do not differ from your deeds. With few desires and contentment, do not covet worldly glory; endure hunger and thirst, setting your will upon non-action (*wuwei*). Diligently study the teachings, cast away all evils, and adorn yourselves with wisdom. Cultivate untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*) to emerge from the sea of birth and death, and further use your wisdom to transform the world according to the truth, leading others to practice the ten wholesome paths. This is what is called saving oneself and saving others, which accords with the work of a Bodhisattva."

At that time, there were bhikṣus in the assembly who, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, reflected upon their own conduct and realized that their actions of body, speech, and mind did not accord with the Dharma. More than five hundred of them immediately rose to pay their respects, prostrated themselves in repentance, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In accordance with the World-Honored One’s instruction, we all possess these three unwholesome karmas.”
Now, before the Buddha, I confess and repent my transgressions.
I pray only that the Celestial Honored One will examine and witness my sincerity.
From this day forward, I vow never again to commit what is wrong, but shall act in accordance with the Dharma.
"May the Buddha bear witness. The Buddha said, "O sons!"
“The Honored One of the Three Realms, Father of sentient beings, your son now repents his evil and cultivates goodness; this is truly a cause for joy, and we shall rejoice with you.
Furthermore, five hundred bhikṣus of coarse conduct, having heard these words, immediately rose to pay their respects and prostrated themselves before the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
We are incapable of practicing the path of renunciation. Why is this?

Since time immemorial, for the sake of gain and offerings, we have practiced crookedness and defilement; being empty yet appearing real, we have accepted the offerings of others until our debts have grown ever more numerous.
"For these reasons, I am truly filled with anxiety and fear.
I now wish to abandon the Way and return to the conditions of secular life; I pray that the Buddha will grant me his hearing.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
“Excellent, excellent!
I join you in your joy. Why is this?
When a person enters into practice, it is like grasping a blade or holding poison; for one who cannot endure it, it is better not to do it at all.
Why is this? Because if one holds onto it without diligence, it will instead bring about harm.
Now that you all believe in karmic retribution and possess a sense of shame and remorse,
by virtue of this shame and remorse, you shall eliminate past transgressions and increase your roots of goodness.
"When Maitreya Bodhisattva later attains Buddhahood, you shall be among those first to attain liberation when he preaches the Dharma.
He further addressed the bhikṣus:
"It would be better to cut the flesh from one's own body to provide sustenance than to accept the offerings of others with a crooked mind."
"It is most difficult, most difficult!
Be cautious, be cautious!

At that time, fifty śrāmaṇeras, including the Buddha’s son Rāhula, having heard the Buddha explain the origins, causes, and full details of the calamities that befell Śaṇḍila and the others, were filled with great anxiety and fear. They immediately paid their respects, prostrating themselves with their heads at the Buddha's feet, and with palms joined, addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Having now heard this teaching on the karmic causes and conditions of the śraddhāhīna and others, and the suffering they undergo as their retributive fruit, I am filled with great fear. Why is this so?

The Upādhyāya Śāriputra possessed great wisdom and merit; he was known and esteemed by the eminent families of the kingdom, such that the multitude vied with one another to assemble like clouds to make offerings, presenting him with the most excellent and delicious delicacies.

This child is foolish and lacks merit; though he has consumed such exquisite and sweet food and drink, in future lives he shall surely repay this karmic cause and condition by suffering the retribution of a śandiha. For this reason, we truly harbor deep anxiety.
Even those five hundred monks of long-standing virtue and great merit were unable to endure it; they have retreated from the Path and returned to lay life, let alone these children who lack wisdom.

We pray that the Buddha will look upon us with compassion and grant permission for us to abandon the Path and return home, so that we may avoid further transgression and escape future suffering and calamity.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Rāhula:
"If you now fear transgression and wish to return home to seek release from suffering, this will not come to pass."

Why is this? It is like two people who, being destitute of food and suffering from hunger, suddenly encounter a host who provides them with various kinds of rich and delicious delicacies; these people, being hungry, greedily eat until they are overfull.
Now, of these two persons, one is wise and the other is foolish.

The wise person, realizing for himself that he has overeaten and that his body is heavy, groaning and yawning, and fearing the onset of suffering and affliction, immediately goes to a skilled physician. With humble and submissive intent, he bows his head in supplication for rescue, entreating the removal of his suffering and affliction.
The skilled physician then bestowed the medicine *māṃtr̥dā* upon him and instructed him to take it; the man immediately vomited up the old food remaining in his stomach.
Once he had vomited the old food, the physician ordered him to stay near a warm fire and to observe strict dietary and lifestyle restrictions.
Because of this, that person escapes calamity and misfortune, ultimately preserving their lifespan in peace, security, and happiness.

Those who lack wisdom do not recognize the excesses of their diet; instead, they claim it is due to demons and spirits, squandering family wealth and needlessly slaughtering living beings to offer sacrifices to ghosts and deities in a vain attempt to save their lives—thus wasting their efforts in vain.

Undigested food remaining in the belly subsequently gives rise to wind; this wind produces cramps and piercing pain in the heart, leading to death and rebirth in the hells. One undergoes suffering for successive lifetimes due to a lack of wisdom.
The Buddha said,
“Rāhula! Your returning home out of fear of punishment is like that of a person who is ignorant and foolish.”

Those who seek merit and wish to be free from transgressions should be humble and diligent, draw near to enlightened teachers, cultivate wisdom, repent of evil karmic deeds, and reform the past while cultivating the future.
From this point on, wisdom will gradually be perfected; because wisdom is perfected, all transgressions are extinguished.
As I have previously stated, just as the power of the sun’s radiance can dispel all darkness, so too is it for a person who cultivates wisdom.

Because you previously possessed the causal conditions of roots of goodness, you have encountered me; just as Śāriputra and others, like that skilled physician, were able to relieve suffering and illness so as not to die, why do you now abandon the light to enter the darkness?
The śrāmaṇera Rāhula addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The wisdom of all Buddhas is like the great ocean, while the minds of Rāhula and others are like the tip of a hair; how could we possibly receive and uphold the wisdom of the Tathāgata?”
The Buddha told Rāhu: "It is like drops of rain falling one after another; though each subsequent drop does not reach the previous one, they together fill a large vessel.

The cultivation of wisdom is also like this: beginning from something small and subtle, it eventually becomes a great vessel. Once it has become a great vessel, it transforms further into other vessels; thus, through successive stages, it fills immeasurable vessels. This is what is called benefiting oneself and benefiting others. One who benefits themselves and benefits others is called a Great Being (Mahāsattva), such as I am now."

Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Rāhula and the others were enlightened in mind and liberated in understanding; they no longer harbored any further anxieties, and would faithfully carry out the World-Honored One’s instructions as taught, not daring to entertain any doubts.

At that time, there was a prince in the assembly named Jeta. Having heard the Buddha’s teaching on the ten paths of wholesome action and how their causes, conditions, and karmic fruits are inexhaustible, he knelt with palms joined and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"In the past, the Buddha instructed me to uphold the five precepts; now I wish to relinquish them and receive the ten paths of wholesome action."
"Why is this? Among the five precepts, the precept against intoxicants is difficult to observe, for one fears incurring transgression.
The World-Honored One replied:
"When you drink wine, what evil is there?
Jeta replied to the Buddha:
"The powerful and influential men of the country often lead one another out, bringing wine and food to enjoy themselves together and achieve pleasure; for me personally, there is no evil."
"Why is this? Because by recollecting the precepts while under the influence of alcohol, one remains free from negligence; therefore, even when drinking alcohol, one does not commit evil.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"Excellent, excellent!
Jeta, you have now attained wisdom and skillful means;
if people in the world were like you, what evil would there be in drinking wine for the rest of one's life?"
A practitioner who acts in this manner shall generate merit and incur no transgression.
Generally, there are two kinds of virtuous conduct for persons:
the first is with outflows (*sāsrava*), and the second is without outflows (*anāsrava*).
As for conditioned wholesome karma, it constantly results in the retribution of happiness among gods and humans;
as for unconditioned wholesome karma, it results in the retribution of nirvana, which transcends the suffering of birth and death.
If a person drinks alcohol, because they do not give rise to a mind of joy that incites evil karma, they do not give rise to afflictions.
Through the causal conditions of a virtuous mind, one receives the retribution of wholesome fruits.
What loss could there be in your upholding of the five precepts?
Even while drinking alcohol, if you remain mindful of the precepts, your merit will increase all the more.
"Previously you observed the five precepts, and now you have received the ten wholesome actions; the merit of this is twice as superior as the retribution for the ten wholesome actions.
At that time, King Prasenajit said to the World-Honored One:
"World-Honored One!"
As the Buddha has taught, when the mind is joyful, one does not give rise to unwholesome karma; this is called "outflowing wholesome" (*sāsrava-kuśala*).

This is not so. Why? When a person drinks alcohol, the mind becomes joyful; because of this joyful mind, afflictions do not arise; because there are no afflictions, one does not commit harm; because one does not harm things, the three karmas are pure; and the path of purity is precisely outflow-free karma (*anāsrava-karma*).
"World-Honored One, please remember: formerly, while I was traveling about for hunting and recreation, I forgot to bring my cook along.

In the deep mountains, becoming hungry and desiring food, those around me replied, 'When Your Majesty departed this morning, you did not issue an order to bring the cook; thus, we have no food at present.'"
Having heard these words, I galloped back to the palace on horseback and ordered that food be sought out.
The royal kitchen superintendent was named Śukara. Śukara said:
"There is no food currently available; it must be prepared now.
At that time, driven by hunger, I was so overcome by rage that I failed to reflect; in my delusion and fury, I commanded an attendant official to execute the kitchen supervisor.
Having received the King’s command, I immediately consulted with my colleagues and said:

"In the entire kingdom, this man alone is loyal, virtuous, and upright in his service. If he were to be killed now, there would be no one else capable of serving as the King's kitchen supervisor to satisfy Your Majesty’s wishes."
At that time, Lady Mallikā, having heard the King’s command to execute Sūkarika, felt great affection for him;

knowing the King was hungry and exhausted, she immediately ordered the preparation of fine meat and excellent wine, bathed herself with famous perfumes, adorned her body, and went to my dwelling accompanied by various female musicians.
When I saw the Lady adorned in magnificent finery, accompanied by her handmaidens and bringing fine wine and meat, my anger immediately subsided. Why was this?
Because the Lady Mallikā observes the Buddha’s five precepts and abstains from drinking alcohol; for this reason, my mind was constantly filled with resentment.

Today, he suddenly brought wine and meat to enjoy together with us, expressing his deep affection; thus, I drank the wine and ate the meat with my wife, performing various musical performances in joyful entertainment, and my heart of resentment was immediately extinguished.
The lady, knowing that I had forgotten my anger, immediately dispatched a eunuch to convey my command, instructing him to tell the outer ministers not to kill the kitchen supervisor.
They immediately carried out her instructions.
When morning dawned, I deeply reproached myself; filled with sorrow and distress, my countenance grew haggard.
My wife asked me:
"For what reason are you so sorrowful? What is your affliction?"
I said: "Because I was oppressed by the fire of hunger yesterday, I killed Śukara out of a mind of anger.
I calculated that there is no one else in the kingdom capable of supervising my kitchen like Śukara; for this reason, I am filled with regret, remorse, and sorrow."
The lady smiled and said, "That man is still alive; I pray the King do not grieve.
I asked her again:
"Is this truly so, or is it a jest?
He replied, "It is indeed so; it is not a false statement."

“I ordered my attendants to summon the chief cook. The messenger went to call him and he was brought here in a short while; I was greatly delighted, and my grief and resentment were immediately dispelled.

The King said to the Buddha, “Lady Mallikā observes the five precepts of the Buddha and practices the six fasts every month. Within a single day, she has violated two of her lifelong five precepts—those against drinking alcohol and false speech—and has suddenly broken six of the eight fast-day precepts.”
"What is this matter?
Is the offense of violating the precepts light or heavy?
The World-Honored One replied:
"Committing such a transgression of the precepts results in great merit and is without fault.
Why is this? Because it is for the sake of benefiting others."
As I have previously stated, there are generally two kinds of wholesome deeds practiced by a person:
first, wholesome deeds with outflows (*sāsrava-kuśala*); second, wholesome deeds without outflows (*anāsrava-kuśala*).
The precept that Queen Mallikā has transgressed falls within the category of wholesome deeds with outflows.
That which does not violate the precepts is called untainted goodness (*anāsrava-kuśala*).
According to the literal meaning of the words, practicing goodness while violating the precepts is called tainted goodness (*sāsrava-kuśala*);
according to the intended meaning of the words, all goodness arising from the ordinary mind is untainted karma.
The King addressed the Buddha, saying:

“As the World-Honored One has taught, if Queen Mallikā, though she drank wine and broke the precepts, gave rise to no evil mind and thus possesses merit and is free from karmic retribution, then all the people likewise should be so.”

Why is this? I recall that not long ago, in the city of Śrāvastī, there were several noble Kṣatriya princes who, due to a minor dispute, came to harbor great resentment. Each plotted against the other and raised armies to punish one another. Both families were prominent lineages within the kingdom and were also relatives; they could not be arrested, and their chaotic fighting did not heed reasoned counsel. I was deeply concerned about this.
He further reflected to himself:

"In the past, when I was a prince, there was a high minister of the former king named Devila. Relying on his noble lineage, wealth, status, and power, he treated me with contempt and mocked me with derision, worse than any beast."
At that time, filled with rage and unable to distinguish right from wrong, he desired to exterminate them but found his strength insufficient;
he appealed to his father, the King, yet the King would not listen or grant him audience.
Bearing poison in my heart and harboring resentment, there was nothing that could be done.
For these reasons, my food and drink diminished from their usual amount, and I was consumed by vexation and sorrow.
At that time, the Empress Dowager saw me in such distress and admonished me in various ways, yet my grief did not cease.
Thereupon, the Empress Dowager, out of deep maternal affection for her son, dispatched a messenger to seek fine wine and urged me to drink it.
I immediately said to my mother:
"Our lineage has been handed down from our ancestors to serve the god Nārāyaṇa and to honor the Brahmins."
"If I were to drink wine now, I fear the wrath of Heaven and the reproaches and punishments of the Brahmins.

At that time, the Empress Dowager, fearing her son might lose his life, closed the palace gates during the quiet hours of the night so that no outsiders, eunuchs, or maidservants could know of it. The Empress Dowager said:
"As for the heavenly deities, they possess a heart of compassion and save all from suffering; the Brahmins should likewise be so."
"My son, you are now suffering in grief and torment; it would be in vain for you to lose your life, for how could even the heavenly deities save your life?
You should rather take medicine to dispel your sorrow and affliction, so that you may preserve both body and life."
"How could these brahmins, who have not yet attained the divine eye, know of their son’s secret affairs?
Though pressured repeatedly, he eventually acquiesced.
Once he had drunk the wine, his grief and resentment were forgotten.

When the Empress Dowager saw her son’s countenance restored, her heart was immediately filled with joy; she summoned the palace women to perform songs and music, and for twenty-one days she enjoyed the pleasures of the five senses, whereby the resentment and anger she had pursued were from that point on stilled.

Having reflected thus, he immediately commanded his loyal ministers to prepare fine wine and various delicacies. He further ordered that a proclamation be made throughout the kingdom for the local elites, high officials, and commoners to assemble all together, as he wished to deliberate upon a great matter of state concerning the rivalries among the ministers.
The two groups of followers, each numbering five hundred, were summoned and assembled; the royal palace was adorned with magnificent music.
The King commanded his loyal ministers to prepare crystal bowls with a capacity of three *sheng*, and to fill various precious bowls to the brim with fine wine.
"I shall eat a bowl first before the assembly.
The King said,
"Now that we discuss the great affairs of the kingdom, I believe you sit in this assembly with no ulterior motives."
"Now each person must prepare one bowl of this ambrosial, excellent medicine; only then shall we discuss the matter.
They all replied, "Yes, sir; we obey the Great King's command."

He then commanded his musicians to perform the Grand Music; when the people received the wine and heard the music, their hearts were filled with joy, they forgot their resentment, and they became carefree and free from sorrow.
The King again held up the bowl and said to the gentlemen:
"When a man cultivates virtue, it is transmitted from generation to generation; one must follow the holy teachings without deviation."
"Gentlemen, why do you contend with such anger over a trivial matter?
If you cannot exercise forbearance, I fear the succession of the state will perish.
For this reason, I urge you earnestly: please cease this dispute."
The ministers replied,
"We respectfully receive your weighty command and dare not disobey.
Thereupon, peace was established.

The king said to the Buddha, “People do not give rise to disputes because of alcohol; rather, it is by obtaining alcohol that they pacify their hearts of anger and contention, thereby attaining great peace.”
Is this not indeed the efficacy of wine?
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

Observe those in the world who are poor and lowly—slaves, servants, and people from the borderlands—who may gather at festivals or in taverns to drink wine; because of their joyful hearts, they each rise to dance without needing anyone to instruct them."
Before one has obtained wine, none of these things exist.

Therefore, one should know that because people drink wine they attain joy; when the mind is joyful, evil thoughts do not arise; when evil thoughts do not arise, this is a virtuous mind; and by reason of a virtuous mind, one ought to receive a virtuous retribution.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
Even a monkey can dance when it obtains wine, let alone a human being.
As the World-Honored One has said, 'Giving good brings a good retribution; giving evil brings an evil retribution.'"
Just as people in the world, by virtue of the causal conditions of merit from previous acts of giving, now attain great wealth;
yet when the poor beg from them, they are stingy and refuse to give, and through these causal conditions of greed and parsimony, they receive the retribution of hungry ghosts.
There are people in the world, whether men or women, who possess upright and handsome forms; those men who are handsome are loved by women, and those women who are beautiful are cherished by men.
If there is someone with great power who forcibly prevents men and women from uniting, and because they cannot unite, they consequently experience sorrow and suffering—
where should the karmic retribution for this transgression fall?
"Venerable Lady Mallikā, it is entirely because she practiced giving generously in her previous lives that she now receives this excellent retribution.
Why does the World-Honored One cause her to observe the five precepts and practice the six fasts every month?"

On the six days of fasting, one must not adorn oneself with fragrant flowers or fine garments; furthermore, one is not permitted to perform songs or play music, nor is one permitted to draw near to the graceful charms that a husband loves. What, then, can be accomplished? One’s efforts are wasted in vain—is this not suffering?
The Buddha said to the king:
"Great King, what you have questioned is indeed as you say.
When Queen Mallikā was young, had I not commanded her to receive the precepts and cultivate wisdom, how could she have attained the virtue she possesses today?"
Since she was able to cross over [the flood] herself and further enabled the King’s body to cross as well, to whom does such merit belong?
Because Queen Mallikā accepted my instruction and acted according to it, she has today accomplished wisdom, skillful means, and liberation.

Furthermore, Great King! It is like a man of the world who has an only son; wishing for him to achieve maturity, when the boy is still young, he takes him to a school and entrusts him to a teacher to instruct him in the arts, writing, and the social graces expected of men. The regulations of the school are all strictly enforced: there are reprimands and corporal punishments, restrictions on food and drink, and prohibitions against sleep. In coming and going, one must not fail to observe the proper decorum; should anyone commit a transgression, punishment is meted out according to the gravity of the offense.

Because the child feared the staff, he applied himself single-mindedly to his studies; by the time he reached adulthood, he possessed such lofty talent and vast learning that there was nothing he did not know, and he in turn used what he knew to teach others.
Lady Mallikā’s observance of the fast and her upholding of the precepts were likewise so.
"Furthermore, Great King!
Just as Pūrṇa, out of a heart of envy and jealousy, severed his bonds of affection, took leave of his parents, abandoned his wife and children, and entered the mountains to practice and study."
Clad in garments of grass, enduring the cold and bearing hardship, he made this vow:
"I shall commit to memory the ninety-six kinds of sutras, records, and treatises until I have mastered them all; if not, I shall not return to see my parents."

After twenty years had passed, he attained complete mastery of all things and returned to the city of Rājagṛha. Carrying a torch upon his head and wrapping his belly with copper plates, he walked along the main road, proclaiming aloud: "I am omniscient!"
He came to where I was and said to me:
"Śramaṇa Gautama, what exactly do you know?
I replied, "Foolish man," and spoke this verse:
"If one has heard even a little and yet is self-important and arrogant toward others, this is like a blind man holding a torch: it illuminates others but does not enlighten himself."

When Pūrṇa heard these words, he was suddenly enlightened in his heart; he cast away the torch, unbound his belly, and prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground in shame and remorse for his transgressions—all because of his extensive learning, wisdom, and sharp faculties.
In the moment before arising, he severed the outflows (*āsrava*) of the three realms and attained the power of wisdom of the path of Arhatship.

Great King, you should know that those who practice study all do so by restraining and governing the five sensory faculties; only then do they attain unimpeded penetration, which is called "unobstructed wisdom" (*anāvaraṇajñāna*). One who possesses unobstructed wisdom is endowed with the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). It is like a trained elephant that turns according to the goad. Great King, you should know that practitioners all rely on restraint to govern the five sensory faculties; thereafter, they achieve thorough penetration without any hindrance, which is termed "unobstructed wisdom. One who possesses unobstructed wisdom is equipped with the four analytical knowledges.
Now, Pūrṇa possesses the four analytical eloquences, all of which were obtained through his diligent study and tireless endurance of hardship.
Therefore, I say that one who possesses wisdom and understanding has seven virtuous qualities.
What are the seven? First, the faculty of faith;

second, the faculty of diligence; third, the faculty of ethical discipline; fourth, the faculty of shame and remorse; fifth, the faculty of learning; sixth, the faculty of equanimity; seventh, the faculty of concentration and wisdom.
These are the seven faculties.
Queen Mallikā is endowed with these seven talents.

Great King, you should know that although Queen Mallikā possesses a female body, her lofty wisdom and broad learning are not like those of ordinary people; this is entirely because from her youth she has been careful in body, speech, and mind, and has single-mindedly and exclusively cultivated wisdom.
"By the power of wisdom it is called liberation; furthermore, through wisdom one brings understanding to the world.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of the novice Rāhula, spoke these verses for the great assembly:
"Hearing is like the golden-winged bird, Whose majesty and martial strength are powerful."
Learning is a treasury of practice, benefiting all wherever one may be;
learning is a great bridge, delivering one from all sufferings and calamities;
learning is a great mariner, ferrying one across the ocean of birth and death.
Much learning makes the will resolute; through resoluteness, wisdom increases.
Wisdom leads to a broad understanding of meanings; one who sees, hears, and practices the Dharma dwells in peace.
Much learning can dispel sorrow and enable one to find joy in meditative concentration.
Skillfully understanding the nectar-like Dharma, one thereby attains Nirvāṇa.
Hearing leads to knowledge of the Vinaya; it resolves doubts and reveals what is right.
Through hearing, one abandons what is not the Dharma, and by practice reaches the deathless state.
The sages honor and learn from this; so too do the devas.
By restraining the mind and avoiding negligence, one accumulates learning to achieve noble wisdom.
Wisdom can dispel sorrow and affliction, and likewise eliminate unwholesome decline.
Those who seek peace and auspiciousness should serve the wise.
By following them, the blind gain sight, as if finding a lamp in the darkness;
they guide the people of the world, like a clear-sighted leader for those without vision.
"Therefore, one should abandon delusion, Leave behind pride and the pleasures of wealth and status, And devote oneself to learning from those who are wise; This is called the accumulation of merit.
When the World-Honored One had spoken this verse, he further addressed the King, saying:

"Your Majesty’s present merit, your keen intelligence, and your broad mastery of principles all result from having personally attended upon enlightened teachers in previous lives, serving them with diligent devotion, and the results of your studies;

through these causes and conditions and their karmic fruition, you have now become a king of men, possessing wisdom so clear and far-reaching that your skillful and appropriate manner of receiving and guiding others is rare indeed in this world."
Therefore, I say that the wisdom of prajñā has four meanings.

For this reason, you should know that those who seek the three vehicles ought to study prajñā; those who wish to escape the sufferings and afflictions of the three evil realms and the eight difficult conditions, and who wish to receive the joyful retributions of humans and devas—in short, all who seek every merit—should cultivate and study wisdom and skillful means.

As I have previously stated, because King Ajita diligently practiced and cultivated the power of wisdom, although he fell into misconduct and was reborn in the evil realms, he constantly maintained the memory of his past lives;

because he remembered his past lives, he reformed his evils and cultivated goodness, swiftly attaining liberation, and moved the various devas to provide him with assistance and offerings, serving as a teacher for the devas through the power of his wisdom.
"For these reasons, I say that there are four meanings of Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, King Prasenajit, having heard from the Buddha this discourse on the causes and conditions of the merit of wisdom and skillful means, was filled with great joy.

Prince Jeta, the queen, the empress dowager, the ministers, the officials, and the common people—all the great assembly were without exception enlightened and understood; each paid their respects by prostrating before the Buddha and returned to their seats as before.
The king joined his palms and said,
“As the Buddha has stated, there are generally two kinds of wholesome deeds practiced by people of the world:
first, wholesome deeds with outflows (sāsrava-kuśala), and second, wholesome deeds without outflows (anāsrava-kuśala).”
“World-Honored One, since the two meanings of ‘with outflows’ and ‘without outflows’ ultimately converge into one,
why do you speak of their distinctions?
The Buddha told the king:
“There are two types of persons:
first, those of sharp faculties; second, those of dull faculties.
For the sake of persons with dull faculties, I teach two kinds of goodness.”
For those of sharp faculties, one does not speak of two.
Why is this? All streams and sources of water ultimately flow back into the single ocean.
"Because those of dull faculties have their senses obscured and blocked, I have taught them the Dharma through analytical distinctions.
At that time, King Jeta, the prince, addressed the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!..."
Is there a distinction among the precepts of the ten wholesome actions,
or are they of the same meaning?
Is the meaning of the precept against false speech the same [as the others]?
"Are there many?
If they constitute a single meaning, it can never be maintained; if they are of different categories, I pray that the Buddha will explain them.
The Buddha told him:
"There are two kinds of false speech:
first, the grave; second, the light.
What is meant by the grave?"

If those who have received the precepts do not cultivate wisdom, being foolish and lacking insight, they will be unable to teach and cause the Buddha-dharma to flourish. For this reason, they are held in contempt by others and fail to receive offerings; being impoverished and suffering, they outwardly manifest diligence for the sake of receiving offerings while inwardly practicing what is perverse and turbid. They successively instruct one another and proclaim to the people:
"The bhikṣu practices asceticism with diligence and has attained the realm of dhyāna."
Some say they have seen the Buddha, some say they have seen dragons, and some say they have seen ghosts.
Such persons are called great liars; those who commit this offense fall into the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, false speech can lead to the killing of people and the destruction of families; moreover, there is false speech that violates agreements and causes others to harbor resentment—this is called the lowest form of false speech.
One who acts in such a manner is said to have violated the precepts and will fall into the minor hells.
As for other forms of frivolous play, as well as various private matters or secret prohibitions—whether one says what does not exist or denies what exists—one does not violate the precepts.
Having heard these words, Prince Jeta immediately received the Dharma of the Ten Paths of Wholesome Action before the Buddha and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Today my doubts and regrets have been eliminated; I have resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. I pray that the Buddha will bear witness to this.”
The Buddha said:
“Excellent! I greatly rejoice; you should know that this is the right time.”
The King addressed the Buddha, saying:

“As the Buddha has taught regarding the causes, conditions, and karmic retributions of sentient beings as understood by the wise and holy ones of the ten directions: my late father, the former king, served non-Buddhist paths and observed their prohibitions, abstaining from wine, meat, the five pungent vegetables, scallions, and garlic;

he made offerings to Brahmā, the sun, the moon, water, and fire; he constantly practiced giving, seeking the merit of Brahmā, and every year regularly bestowed a thousand milch cows upon the Brahmins—calculated over forty years, this amounts to forty thousand cows.”
"O Brahmins, you consume the flavors of milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, and the finest essence (mṛdvīkā).
By such merit, in which heaven will you be reborn?"
"I pray that the Buddha will compassionately grant us detailed instruction so that all practitioners may universally hear and understand it.
The Buddha told the king:
"The former king’s karmic retribution is currently within hell."
Why is this so? Because one has failed to encounter a favorable time, failed to meet virtuous friends, and lacked skillful means, one cannot escape retribution for offenses despite cultivating merit.
The merit of giving is not lost; once the period of retribution for the offenses has ended, one shall then receive the blessings.
"Great King, you should know that when a person cultivates merit, it does not coincide with sin. Because they do not coexist, one must employ skillful means to ensure that the sin is extinguished.
What are these skillful means?"
This refers to a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra). What is meant by a virtuous friend?
It is one who possesses right view; such a person is a virtuous friend, for they constantly discipline the mind through correct teaching.

What is meant by the "Right Teaching"? It refers to contemplating impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; observing how the twelve links of dependent origination entangle one in birth and death; cultivating the Four Noble Truths—seeing suffering, severing its origin, realizing its cessation, and practicing the path; and practicing the six *pāramitās* and the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*). These are the skillful means for subduing the sense faculties. Because the faculties are subdued, concentration and wisdom are perfected. Because wisdom is perfected, the mind becomes upright. Because the mind is upright, one is able to arouse diligence. Because of a diligent mind, one is able to give rise to conscientious restraint. When conscientious restraint reaches its ultimate, concentration and wisdom become clear and lucid.

Because their wisdom is clear and lucid, they traverse all myriad practices with unimpeded penetration; because their conduct is unimpeded, it is called liberation, and the liberated mind is itself nirvana.
This is what is meant by a "good spiritual friend."
"Great King, you should know that a wise teacher who provides skillful guidance is a great causal condition that must not be taken lightly.

That you have now encountered a worthy one and met a sage is entirely due to the karmic fruits and conditions of your past lives; having heard the Dharma, you have gained faith and understanding, and are further able to explain it to others."
Therefore, I say that it is difficult to encounter a person of wisdom, and such a one does not exist everywhere; wherever they are born, their kinsmen and relatives receive blessings.
For this reason, you should cultivate the wisdom of Prajñā.
The king addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Having heard the World-Honored One’s discourse on wisdom and skillful means, they have all penetrated my heart.
As the World-Honored One has said, misfortune and fortune are not the same."
"What evil karma did my late father, the Great King, commit that he must now undergo this retribution?
The Buddha told the king:
"The late Great King committed six kinds of offenses."
What are the six types?
First, being arrogant and maliciously envious, one inflicts lashes and punishments regardless of whether a matter is major or minor, because one lacks forbearance.
Second, coveting precious goods, one adjudicates matters unfairly, thereby causing the people of the world to harbor resentment.
Third, because they engage in hunting and frivolous play, causing hardship and distress to the people and harming the dear lives of sentient beings.
Fourth, because they confine their palace women, depriving them of their will and causing them to undergo great suffering.
Fifth, because they are addicted to female beauty, becoming weary of the old upon obtaining the new, and treating others with partiality, thereby causing resentment;
sixth, because they fear the Brahmins and thus steal food, wine, meat, and the five pungent herbs—scallions and garlic—acting with deceit for fear of being rebuked.
"These are the six matters; through the causal conditions of such sinful karma, one is born in the hells.
The King addressed the Buddha, saying, "If this is so, then before the Buddha appeared in the world, his disciples also possessed such sins; what should have been done in that case?"
"By practicing the ten wholesome actions, one may achieve them without obstruction?
The Buddha told the king:
"As I have previously said, when the sun rises, all darkness is extinguished; is there any remaining darkness left?"
The king said, “If even the light of a lamp can extinguish darkness, how much more so the power and majesty of the sun’s radiance?

[The Buddha replied,] “Now, by virtue of your merit, O King, having heard the Buddha’s teaching and attained wisdom, you are like the sunlight that extinguishes all darkness, leaving no remaining faults.”

The King addressed the Buddha, saying: “The brahmin teachers whom my father served were diligent and wise, practicing asceticism; for the sake of seeking merit, they did not spare their own bodies or lives. Some threw themselves from cliffs or scorched their bodies with the five fires; some abstained from food and drink, seeking rebirth in the Brahma Heaven; some piled up great heaps of firewood and burned their own bodies alive; some stood on one leg with mouths agape facing the sun; some tied their feet with ropes to high trees and suspended themselves upside down; some lay upon beds of thorns or embraced stones to beat their chests. Such were the various kinds of ascetic practices they performed.”
"To what do the merits of asceticism and the causal conditions of merit lead?
The Buddha answered him, saying:
"As I have previously taught, practicing suffering results in the retribution of suffering; practicing pleasure results in the retribution of pleasure."
“Have you not heard?
The king said, “World-Honored One, did you not establish the precepts for your disciples, requiring them to observe prohibitions? Is this not suffering?”

When a person is hungry and does not immediately obtain food, afflictions arise abruptly and anger becomes intense; being unaware of this state, they give rise to hatred and harbor malice, killing Sūkarika. Since such an act leads to suffering for many lifetimes, is it not indeed evil?
The Buddha told the king:

"The reason I previously established the rule against eating before midday was so that the bhikṣus might abandon the practices of external paths and leave the household life to cultivate the Way within my Dharma."

Having previously practiced asceticism with a mind accustomed to hunger, he obtained rich and delicious food from his disciples; through excessive greed for food, he ate until full, and because the food was not digested, it brought about various illnesses.
Therefore, the regulation of eating was established not for the sake of seeking merit through the suffering of hunger.

Furthermore, those who moderate their food did so because they saw that various bhikṣus were begging indiscriminately day and night without regard for the proper timing of meals, leading to the derision and reproach of non-Buddhists who said:
"The śramaṇa Gautama claims his Way is pure; why does he not follow the methods of the non-Buddhists?"
Therefore, one should practice moderation in eating; it is not for the sake of seeking merit through the suffering of hunger.
To state the essential point: the prohibitions and precepts are established precisely for the foolish who lack skillful wisdom, and not for the wise who understand the appropriate timing.
"As I have previously stated, the wisdom of *prajñā* is itself liberation; it is that which is received by the wise and the sphere of practice for the noble ones.
Having heard this, the King was filled with even greater joy and rose again to pay homage to the Buddha with deep reverence;
the entire assembly did likewise.
King Prasenajit knelt with his palms joined and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"Now this great assembly, having heard what the Buddha has spoken, has had the knots of their web of doubt untied; it is as if the light of the sun has dispelled the darkness, allowing them to see the great radiance."
Such merit as this makes its grace difficult to repay.
By what means, O disciples, should you provide offerings to repay the profound kindness of the World-Honored One in this present life?
The Buddha told the king:
"For you and the entire assembly, the merit of this teaching of the Dharma, which is like nectar, is difficult to repay.

Suppose there were someone who, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, served the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha with all their heart, providing them with clothing, food, bedding, and medicine for illness."
"What do you think? Is that merit great or not?
The King replied, "It is very great; it cannot be measured."
The Buddha told the king:

"The Dharma of Ambrosia is exquisite and beyond measure; it delivers all beings without distinction of coarse or fine, and its merit cannot be repaid by the power of the blessings and virtue of gods or men."
There is only one thing that can repay the Buddha’s kindness.
What is this one thing?

It is to constantly employ a mind of compassion to take all the wholesome dharmas one has understood and, through successive stages, transform and enlighten even a single person, causing them to achieve faith and wisdom; to continue teaching and transforming others without end, just as a single lamp ignites countless other lamps.
A practitioner who acts in this way is said to repay the profound kindness of their teacher and fellow disciples.

Great King, you should know that one who wishes to repay the kindness of their teacher and fellow disciples in attaining liberation must, in turn, liberate sentient beings through wisdom. One who practices in this manner is making offerings to all Buddhas of the three periods of time; it is not merely an offering to repay a single teacher.
The king joined his palms and said:
"If one proclaims the holy teaching to enlighten all living beings, causing them to practice right view and cultivate the noble path, what kind of merit does this produce?"
“I only pray that you will show compassion and guide sentient beings.
The Buddha told the king:

“If a son or daughter of good family hears even a single phrase or a single meaning of the Dharma from a teacher, and through successive teaching and transformation brings it to even one person—causing those who have not yet believed to believe, and those who have not yet understood to understand—the merit of such an act is immeasurable and boundless; it is beyond the capacity of ordinary people to comprehend.”
"Great King!

Suppose there were someone who, for a thousand years, provided food, drink, medicine, and exquisite clothing to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the noble Saṅgha, honoring and revering them with offerings—would their merit not be great?"
The King said, "It is very much, beyond measure.
The Buddha said:

“Great King! If a son or daughter of good family hears the true teaching of the Buddhas from a teacher and proceeds to teach and transform others, even down to a single person, causing them to gain faith and understanding, the merit they obtain will exceed that of the former by many thousands of millions of times; the latter cannot equal even a ten-thousandth part of the former.”
"Why is this? Because the merit of the Dharma-transformation should be immeasurable.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If one diligently proclaims and transforms all people with such a teaching as this, their merit shall be immeasurable. Ānanda!
I now entrust this unsurpassed, wondrous Dharma to you; to proclaim and transform it so as to deliver sentient beings is to make offerings to all Buddhas."
Ānanda joined his palms and addressed the World-Honored One, saying,
“Regarding this sūtra entrusted by the Buddha, what should it be named?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This sutra teaching is titled the *Adbhuta-dharmaparyāya-nidāna-sūtra*; you should diligently practice it.

At that time, King Prasenajit, Prince Jeta, the queen, the ladies of the inner court, the fourfold assembly of disciples, Śakra and Brahmā and the various devas, and the eight classes of nāgas and spirits—eighty thousand people in all—hearing what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced. Each resolved their minds toward the three gates of liberation, prostrated to the Buddha, took their leave, and practiced according to the Dharma.
